articles.summary: The lawmakers say the President must 'take decisive action in response to statements and conduct that undermine national sovereignty and threaten the country's security'

blocks.text: LOWER CHAMBER. The House of Representatives Session Hall.
House of Representatives' Facebook page
The lawmakers say the President must 'take decisive action in response to statements and conduct that undermine national sovereignty and threaten the country's security'

items: Ten House lawmakers in the Philippines filed House Resolution No. 1562 urging President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. to declare Chinese Ambassador Jing Quan persona non grata or request his recall from Beijing.
The resolution was prompted by Jing's controversial statement perceived as a threat to the Philippines, alongside the Chinese Embassy's dismissive response to the lawmakers' concerns.
The lawmakers emphasized the need for decisive action to protect national sovereignty and criticized the Chinese Embassy's language as undiplomatic and arrogant.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MANILA, Philippines – Ten House lawmakers filed a proposed resolution urging President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. to either declare Chinese Ambassador Jing Quan persona non grata or ask Beijing to recall him.

House Senior Deputy Minority Leader Leila de Lima (Mamamayang Liberal) and House Assistant Minority Leader Chel Diokno (Akbayan) joined eight other lawmakers in authoring House Resolution No. 1562, filed on Wednesday, October 21.
Their move followed similar resolutions filed in the upper chamber by senators Erwin Tulfo and Risa Hontiveros.
Other lawmakers who signed the House resolution are:

items: House Assistant Majority Leader and Lanao del Sur 1st District Representative Zia Adiong
House Assistant Majority Leader and Las Pinas Representative Mark Santos
Zamboanga del Norte 3rd District Representative Adrian Michael Amatong
Pinoy Workers Representative Karl Legazpi
House Deputy Minority Leader and Akbayan Representative Perci Cendana
House Deputy Minority Leader and Dinagat Islands Representative Kaka Bag-ao
House Deputy Minority Leader and Albay 1st District Representative Krisel Lagman
Akbayan Representative Dadah Ismula

blocks.text: “Under the Constitution, the President, being vested with foreign power, holds primary authority to conduct foreign relations and to represent the nation in its dealings with other states, and must therefore take decisive action in response to statements and conduct that undermine national sovereignty and threaten the country’s security,” the proposed resolution read.

The lawmakers cite a number of incidents that led to the filing of the resolution, starting with Jing’s October 15 statement saying that if China wants to use force, “we may easily win.” Philippine government officials, including the President, later said the statement sounded like a threat.

The Chinese Embassy dared the Senate and the House to just declare Jing as persona non grata and “stop bluffing.” It also threatened to block Philippine officials from entering China if Jing were to be declared persona non grata.

Before the group of House lawmakers filed the resolution, they sounded the alarm over Jing’s seeming threat against the Philippines, and the Chinese embassy’s subsequent language that seemed dismissive of Filipinos’ sentiments.

“The embassy’s undiplomatic language taunting our government to declare the Chinese ambassador as persona non grata does little to encourage serious dialogue between two sovereign nations. Instead it reflects their position that our country should simply accept China’s threats and submit to its demands,” they said.
“The Philippines must not be cowed into silence in the face of such arrogance,” the lawmakers added. – Rappler.com

articles.title: UK approves Jackdaw gasfield in North Sea
articles.summary:
Decision was widely expected after lobbying by Shell but will dismay environmental campaigners

The UK government has approved the controversial Jackdaw gasfield in the North Sea, a widely…

blocks.text: The UK government has approved the controversial Jackdaw gasfield in the North Sea, a widely expected move that will nonetheless dismay environmental campaigners and a number of Labour MPs.

While Labour’s 2024 election manifesto committed to a ban on new drilling licences in the North Sea, the companies behind Jackdaw and the Rosebank oilfield project, which is being decided on separately, have sought environmental approval for existing licences.

The companies resubmitted their applications for environmental approval earlier this year. The decision on Jackdaw had been expected last month but was delayed, seemingly to take it beyond the Holborn and St Pancras byelection on 8 October, where Labour was defending a seat against a Green challenge and ultimately won.
The Jackdaw field will start supplying gas to homes and businesses from the end of the month, the government said after approving the scheme.

Announcing the decision, the energy secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, said: “Following careful consideration of all relevant factors I have agreed that the regulator can grant consent for gas to be produced at Jackdaw, which will begin to supply the UK with gas from this winter thanks to the highly skilled and vital North Sea workers.

“This decision will support the country’s energy security with homegrown gas this winter and help minimise the UK’s use of imported higher emission fuels as we continue our transition to renewables and nuclear.
“The decision is compatible with our legally binding climate commitments, and we remain resolute in ending new licences for oil and gas and achieving net zero by 2050.”

blocks.caption: Miatta Fahnbulleh, the energy security. Photograph: Marcin Nowak/Anadolu/Getty Images

blocks.text: Environmental campaigners have called for Jackdaw and Rosebank to be abandoned, while Donald Trump has urged Andy Burnham to open them.

Tessa Khan, the executive director of the anti-oil campaign group Uplift, said: “Jackdaw will provide around just 2% of our gas demand for roughly 10 years. It has been oversold and won’t stop the overall decline in North Sea jobs, as it will be largely unmanned and operated remotely.”
She added: “Labour’s climate credibility is on the line. No new oil and gasfields are compatible with safe climate limits.”
The oil and gas industry says the fields will provide 10% of the UK’s output at their peak. But campaigners say they will cause so much environmental damage as to obliterate any economic benefit.

Jackdaw is operated by Shell, and Rosebank by the Norwegian firm Equinor. Both have licences to operate, but environmental approval was rescinded after a judge ruled that the companies needed to account for the carbon emissions that would be created by burning the oil and gas they produce.

The companies have been lobbying hard for the green light. Adura, a North Sea joint venture between Shell and Equinor, commissioned a report this week that said rejecting the two projects would cost the UK economy nearly £10.8bn over the next decade.
The Jackdaw announcement could boost Labour’s position in north-east Scotland, where much of the industry is based and where unions have been campaigning heavily for the permits to be granted.
But it is likely to cause angst among some Labour MPs, especially those in seats where they face a challenge from the Green party.

A poll by Savanta for the climate group E3G and seen by the Guardian shows that nearly a third of voters say they would be less likely to vote Labour if it gives the go-ahead for more North Sea oil drilling.
That includes almost exactly a third of those who voted Labour at the last election, and around half of 18- to 24-year-olds.
Ellie Mae O’Hagan, the UK energy programme lead at E3G, said: “After a summer of deadly heatwaves, the public has made up its mind: more drilling is the wrong answer.

“If the prime minister wants a decade in power to change the country, he should invest in heat pumps and solar, not tax breaks for the oil and gas companies driving up our bills and polluting the planet.”

The Green party leader, Zack Polanski, called the decision “climate vandalism”. He said: “Today’s decision by Labour is a betrayal of all of our futures, Labour has abandoned all credibility in the fight against climate change.

“The energy secretary has herself said it will make no difference to energy bills, the health secretary has admitted the summer heatwave added to pressure on the NHS and the industry’s own assessment is that will create only 27 jobs. This is a victory for Shell over the people.”

blocks.text: MUSK'S SPACEX. SpaceX's logo and an Elon Musk photo are seen in this illustration created on December 19, 2022.
Dado Ruvic/Reuters

items: Elon Musk expressed that merging SpaceX and Tesla could be beneficial, with special committees formed to explore this possibility, leading to an 8% rise in shares.

Elon Musk said on Tuesday, October 20, that a merger of his two companies SpaceX and Tesla would be “a good idea” and that they had formed special committees to discuss a union, sending shares of the space and technology company up 8% in extended trading.

The company earlier posted its first profit as a public company and Musk said he expected annual recurring revenue of between $500 billion and $1 trillion by the end of 2027, as demand for its data-center space surges thanks to the AI boom.

Musk has in the past tantalized shareholders with the idea of combining SpaceX and Tesla, citing growing overlap between them. Speculation about the space company buying the EV maker has gained traction recently, with Barclays suggesting last week that a deal could be announced before Tesla’s annual meeting in December.

“I think it would be a good idea, but it’s really up to the special committees of both companies,” Musk said in the first official confirmation that the companies were formally talking. “Because I’m a conflicted party, I can’t actually be in the discussions of the special committees,” which comprised independent directors, he told investors on a conference call.
The companies had formed the special committees at the request of shareholders, who ultimately would need to approve a deal, he added.

“I do think there’s a lot of merit to combining the companies as we are pretty much in the superintelligence singularity, and there’s a lot to be gained from cooperating on developing superintelligence software, chip design, the Terafab obviously, robotics, mass-to-orbit with the Starmind constellation, connectivity,” he said.

Terafab, the chip manufacturing joint venture between the two companies, should produce its first test chip around May or June of next year and aims to reach volume production by the third quarter of 2028, Musk said on the call.

Musk added that it would be premature to assume a SpaceX-Tesla merger would happen, noting that the special committees had not agreed on transaction terms and may never do so. Tesla shares rose 1.8% in extended trading.
The world’s richest person, Musk owns nearly a fifth of Tesla and just under half of SpaceX, and analysts have said a merger would give him control of the combined entity.

The talks started in recent weeks and could result in SpaceX acquiring Tesla, a person familiar with the matter told Reuters, who declined to be named because they were not authorized to talk to media. Tesla has been working with an investment bank to advise on the discussions, the person said.

SpaceX’s revenue climbed 161% to $14.58 billion for the three months ended September 30 from a year earlier. AI revenue surged by almost 10 times to $7.56 billion, mostly from renting out data-center capacity to developers such as Anthropic, Alphabet’s Google, and Reflection AI rather than from its own models.

The third quarter offered the clearest evidence yet that SpaceX’s heavy investment in AI is translating into revenue, even as spending on compute infrastructure remains enormous — capital expenses nearly tripled to $19.6 billion.

The shift is reshaping a company whose financial engine has long been its Starlink internet services business and whose longer-term ambitions still hinge on getting Starship rockets into regular service. For now, though, its main business looks closer to a cloud provider’s than an AI lab’s.
SpaceX’s chief financial officer, Bret Johnsen, said the company expects $35 billion to $40 billion in capital expenditure in the fourth quarter.

“SpaceX delivered the quarter the bulls wanted, at least on the top line,” said Will Rhind, CEO of asset manager GraniteShares. “The story now is all about AI. The compute contracts signed earlier this year are turning into revenue faster than a lot of people thought.”
The company’s AI business spans Grok, social media platform X, and a fast-growing data-center operation. The business also turned a profit in the third quarter, compared with a year-ago loss.

SpaceX reported net income of $4.4 billion versus a net loss of $1.1 billion a year earlier and analysts’ expectation for a profit of $1.57 billion. On a per-share, adjusted basis, it earned 45 cents according to IBES calculations, outstripping a 13-cent average estimate.

The satellite-internet unit has continued to expand its subscriber base, aided by additional satellite launches and a growing range of consumer, enterprise, aviation, maritime and government services.

Starlink reached 13.6 million subscribers in the third quarter, above the 12.19 million analysts expected, but growth is coming at a price: average monthly revenue per subscriber has fallen from $99 in 2023 to $69 in the third quarter as it expands abroad with cheaper plans.
The company has said geographic expansion beyond the wealthiest countries could push average revenue per user lower over time.

Starship, SpaceX’s next-generation reusable rocket system, has yet to enter commercial service. It is expected to enable deployment of higher-bandwidth Starlink satellites and orbital AI-computing infrastructure. The company’s ability to turn Starship into a reliably reusable vehicle is central to its longer-term strategy.
The space segment includes commercial launches, government missions and Starship development and remains a significant source of costs and uncertainty. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Jess Phillips hopes supreme court ‘sees sense’ and overturns domestic abuse ruling
articles.summary:
Court of appeal decision prevents woman from suing police and CPS for disclosing her address to violent ex-partner

The Labour MP Jess Phillips has said she hopes the UK’s highest court “sees…

blocks.text: The Labour MP Jess Phillips has said she hopes the UK’s highest court “sees sense” and overturns a ruling preventing a domestic abuse survivor from suing Sussex police and the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) for disclosing her address to her violent ex-partner.

Phillips said that if the supreme court upheld the court of appeal’s decision when it hears the case on Wednesday and Thursday, it would prevent police from being held accountable for failures in cases of violence against women and girls.

The address of the woman, anonymised as XGY in court proceedings, was disclosed by a CPS lawyer during a magistrates hearing in which a condition was sought preventing her former partner, who was accused of raping her and threatening to kill and throw acid on her, from entering the road where she was living. Sussex police had not marked the address as confidential when sending it to the CPS. The woman moved home as a result of the disclosure.

Witnesses and lawyers in court traditionally have what is known as “core immunity”. Ruling last year that XGY could not sue Sussex police and the CPS, the court of appeal said this immunity applied beyond evidential matters and also to a broad range of police activity, including matters outside the courtroom relating to an investigation.

Phillips, a former minister for safeguarding and violence against women and girls, said: “Hopefully the supreme court will see sense. I’ve been part of many different cases, where both the police and the CPS, have been held accountable in civil remedy, regarding their failures.

“This isn’t just that I want people to be able to make financial claims against the police. Often these cases where there’s been failures lead to longer-term change for victims of domestic abuse and sexual violence, like police failures within the grooming cases for example – charging women with crimes rather than helping them as victims.
“Criminal law in cases of domestic abuse has seen decades of failure so civil law is used to try and make the systems better and nowhere more so than in violence against women and girls.”

She stressed that it was for the supreme court to reach its own decision but, along with fellow MPs David Davis and Andrew Mitchell, Phillips has tabled an amendment to a bill that would counteract the effect of the court of appeal’s ruling if it was not overturned, as it created “a precedent that was never intended by parliament”.

She said if there was one agency that had improved its approach to violence against women over the past 20 years it was the police but described the court of appeal ruling as “chilling”, adding: “I don’t think it helps the police or the CPS. I don’t think the idea that they can’t be held accountable is something that they need at the moment or should want because there’s a real problem with how victims of domestic abuse perceive the police.

“Inquiry after inquiry, the Sarah Everard murder, Charing Cross [the police station where officers were filmed making racist and misogynistic comments], there are reasons why women don’t have faith in the police and that’s not good for the police and it’s not good for change in the future. So I don’t want to see a sort of really wide-ranging exemption for police to be held accountable with civil action.”
XGY said: “More than six years later, I’m still living with the impact of what happened and the loss of the security I thought I’d finally found.

“I’ve continued with this case because I believe survivors should be able to trust that the information they share to protect themselves will be kept confidential. If that trust is broken, there should be accountability.”
The CPS and Sussex police were approached for comment.

He was indicted by a federal grand jury in Florida last month for selling more than five million counterfeit shipping labels to thousands of US customers over the years. Authorities have now shut down the website.
Earlier this month, the US Postal Inspection Service offered a reward of up to $100,000 for information leading to his arrest.
According to the US Attorney's Office for the Southern District of Florida, the 33-year-old from Khanewal, Pakistan, operated LabelsBank.com.
US prosecutors alleged that he sold counterfeit US postage at a fixed rate regardless of a package's weight, size or destination.

The counterfeit labels, usually sold at $2 each, allegedly allowed customers to ship packages at rates far below legitimate prices, resulting in substantial lost revenue and shipping costs to the Postal Service.
An investigation found that more than 5,200 individuals purchased more than 5.1 million counterfeit shipping labels, the office said in a press release.

Akram is charged with one count of conspiracy to defraud the United States and to make and sell counterfeit postage stamps, five counts of making and selling counterfeit postage stamp labels, and four counts of wire fraud.
If convicted, he faces a maximum penalty of five years in prison on the conspiracy and counterfeit postage counts, and 20 years in prison on each wire fraud count, the office said.

items: Taiwan's National Security Bureau reported that China disseminated over 2.5 million pieces of disputed information targeting Taiwan in the first nine months of 2026, marking a 48% increase from the previous year.
The disinformation campaign focuses on key issues like energy, food security, and defense policy, aiming to influence the upcoming local elections in Taiwan.

China is utilizing AI technology and various online tactics, including fake accounts and coordinated comment flooding, to manipulate information and affect voter preferences ahead of Taiwan's elections.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

TAIPEI, Taiwan – China spread more than 2.5 million pieces of disputed or false online information targeting Taiwan in the first nine months of this year, the island’s top intelligence agency said, accusing Beijing of stepping up operations ahead of local elections.

In a report to lawmakers this week, Taiwan’s National Security Bureau said such information rose by about 48% in the first nine months of 2026 to more than 2.5 million items, from more than 1.69 million a year earlier.

It said the China-originated content focused on energy, food security and defense policy, as well as the platforms and images of specific candidates, in an effort to influence Taiwan’s elections for city mayors and county magistrates in November.

blocks.caption: [DECODED] When the ‘common threat’ is in our midst

blocks.text: China’s Taiwan Affairs Office did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Beijing, which views Taiwan as its own territory over the island’s objections, has previously denied interfering in Taiwanese elections or spreading disinformation.

Taiwan has repeatedly complained about what it sees as China’s “gray-zone” tactics — from daily military drills to cyberattacks — at a time when Beijing is ramping up military and political pressure to force Taipei to accept its sovereignty claims.

The report said Beijing often created narratives through official media outlets before amplifying them through “online troll armies” and public relations firms to sow discord among Taiwanese people. It said the tactics included content farms, AI-generated videos, fake accounts and coordinated comment flooding.
“China has expanded the use of AI technology to manipulate information, seeking to influence voter support and election results,” the report said.

China was using AI technology to gather information on Taiwanese current affairs, candidates’ policies and polling data to shape influence operations and expand AI-driven information manipulation aimed at “affecting voter preferences and election outcomes,” the bureau said.
It said the messages were mainly distributed on social media platforms including Facebook, Threads, YouTube and online forums.

Chinese state media have increasingly amplified Taiwanese critics of the ruling Democratic Progressive Party in an information war, including influencers and politicians linked to the opposition Kuomintang, a Reuters investigation conducted with Taipei-based research group IORG found.

Chinese cyberattacks on Taiwanese government agencies averaged 2.58 million a day in the first nine months of 2026, with detected threats surging from June and reaching 185.6 million in July and 106.4 million in August, data from the National Security Bureau showed.
“It cannot be ruled out that this was advance intelligence-gathering and harassment preparation aimed at interfering in Taiwan’s year-end ‘nine-in-one’ elections,” the report said. – Rappler.com

articles.title: SILG Remulla flags 'new trend' by scammers
articles.summary: Scammers are now operating in smaller units by renting small houses, which is a “new trend,” said Interior Secretary Jonvic Remulla on Wednesday.

blocks.text: Published October 21, 2026 1:35pm
Scammers are now operating in smaller units by renting small houses, which is a “new trend,” said Interior Secretary Jonvic Remulla on Wednesday.
Remulla said that they are going after the so-called “micro hubs” one by one.

“But the new trend is that they are micro hubs of 10 to 15 to 20 who stay in one house. It's not like before. Before, what we had here, the industry had 5,000 people in one building. Now they rent small houses and we are after them,” he said in a press briefing.
Among the recent operations the local authorities conducted against a micro hub was in Zamboanga Sibugay. But the Interior chief said that most of these smaller scam hubs are in the metro area.
“They're mostly operating now here in the metro area. I think we are tracking three active scam hubs. But the exact location is yet to be determined,” said Remulla.
The official said that they are tracking these hubs through electricity and internet consumption, as well as movement of suspicious individuals.
Remulla said that the usual victims of these micro hubs are elderly people.
“What is unfortunate is that we have to step up enforcement because the majority of the victims are senior citizens whose savings are decimated because of these hubs,” said Remulla.
When asked who are the people behind these micro scam hubs, Remulla said that foreigners have local partners here in the country.
“We have identities of the persons and their movements,” he said.
“Foreigners and locals also. They have local partners,” Remulla added. —VAL, GMA News

articles.title: AFP warns Australia of ‘tsunami of youth crime’ and radicalisation accelerated by AI
articles.summary:
Children as young as 12 among dozens subject to federal police operations since 2020, parliamentary inquiry hears

Australia is facing a “tsunami” of youth crime as artificial intelligence…

blocks.text: Australia is facing a “tsunami” of youth crime as artificial intelligence accelerates the pace and scale of radicalisation, a parliamentary inquiry has heard.

The Australian federal police acting deputy commissioner Sandra Booth told the hearing on Wednesday that, while radicalisation had traditionally taken years or months, that process could now happen within days.
“This can be attributed to artificial intelligence, a growing grievance generation, young people searching for purpose and belonging, and the sophistication of these online networks,” she said.
“The AFP is deeply concerned that AI is accelerating and lowering the skills required to actively manipulate and radicalise victims online, and then cause serious harm.”
Booth warned that, without serious intervention, Australia’s mental health, education and judicial systems could be overwhelmed by people committing serious criminal offences.
This may have serious consequences for democracy and institutions.
“Australia is at the crossroads of a tsunami of youth crime as young, vulnerable and impressionable individuals are being radicalised and manipulated at rapid speed,” Booth said.
The country had experienced an increase in the number of threats being made against politicians.
In one example of radicalisation, an investigation found a 13-year-old boy allegedly possessed violent extremist material.
He was using the social media platform Discord and, during a raid at his home, police allege they found a notebook that contained plans for a school shooting.
“This was not in the US,” Booth told the hearing. “This was in Australia.”
The Asio deputy director general for intelligence service delivery, Claire McGuinness, said the spy agency was encountering more children, including 12-year-olds.

“This is in stark contrast to where we were, say, 20 years ago, where we would have seen a caseload predominantly of individuals within their early 20s, so quite a significant shift over the period,” she said.
The inquiry heard since 2020, 65 children, including as young as 12, had been subject to federal police operations.
Thirty-five of those had been charged with state or commonwealth terrorism-related offences.
Intelligence and security committee chair Senator Raff Ciccone said the parliament was trying to understand why people were being radicalised in a matter of days and weeks.
“I want to extend an invitation to people who have been personally affected by radicalisation,” he said.
“We recognise that these experiences can be deeply difficult and that coming forward may not be easy.”
Home affairs department counter‑terrorism coordinator, Brendan Dowling, said the nation was “probably identifying people too late” after they had already come to the attention of law enforcement.
“We’ve long faced an enduring threat from terrorism and violent extremism in Australia but the nature of that threat is changing,” he said.
“It is both more urgent and more challenging than ever before.”
A final report from the parliamentary joint committee on intelligence and security will be handed down in March next year.

articles.title: ‘A difficult line’: meet the editors tackling Wikipedia’s arms trade pages
articles.summary:
Volunteers and new recruits come together for ‘wikithon’ to put more detail about industry into public domain

“Anyone can edit Wikipedia,” the adage goes. But, it turns out, a relatively…

blocks.text: “Anyone can edit Wikipedia,” the adage goes. But, it turns out, a relatively small number actually do.

What is worthy of a digital page in the world’s largest and most-read encyclopedia is decided by roughly 270,000 active volunteers, enthusiasts who populate the online resource with information on anything from 19th-century medicine to TikTok trends. Inevitably, some subjects are sidelined – the global south, notable women – but a new batch of Wikipedian recruits are waging war on one neglected topic: the arms industry.

Last week, in a classroom in central London, two dozen volunteers huddled around laptops and free servings of vegan Ethiopian food for what is known as a “wikithon”, an event of collective and in-person Wikipedia editing. Some were veteran editors in their 70s, others young students who had never registered an account before. But their targets include subjects such as Palantir, Project Maven and Nitro-Chem.

“Wikipedia pages about the arms industry, in general, are not always super-detailed,” said the group’s co-founder Agnes Cameron. The intention of the wikithon, started by fellows from the n-Space programme at Somerset House Studios, was “to put better quality and more well organised information on the arms industry in the public domain”, the specialist technician said.

blocks.caption: A new batch of Wikipedian recruits were trained in how to edit a page.  Photograph: Lily Renshaw/The Guardian

blocks.text: Attenders at the monthly event are trained in how to add to the internet’s most popular reference site. But while editing Wikipedia is surprisingly simple – just a few clicks to publish a change – ethical complications quickly bubble up.
“The interesting thing about Wikipedia editing is that you’re encouraged to edit things you care about,” Cameron said. “What it looks like to have a conflict of interest is an interesting question.”
Although Cameron enjoys editing pages about food in her spare time, her interests are also political. “We’re toeing quite a difficult line,” she said. “Difficult lines are important to toe.”

Despite personal and political reasons for wanting to spread information on arms manufacturers and sellers, finding journalistic balance means using Wikipedia in good faith. Cameron said attenders’ chosen subject matter meant that it was “really important” that they followed Wikipedia’s standards to the letter. “This is not an anti-arms industry campaigning event. This is an event really about factual information on Wikipedia,” she said.

blocks.caption: The main goal was to pull together publicly available information into one place. Photograph: Lily Renshaw/The Guardian

blocks.text: When it comes to information, Wikipedia’s rules demand that no original research is included on its pages and conclusions are not drawn. The main goal of the arms industry wikithon, then, was to pull together publicly available information from other sources into one place.

Wikipedia has been repeatedly criticised for its lack of diversity in editors and its coverage. It has been accused of geographical bias towards the west, with most articles focused on the US and western Europe. Similarly, just 19% of the site’s biography entries are for women. In 2018, the female Nobel prize winner Donna Strickland, a physicist, was deemed “not important enough” for a Wikipedia entry.

With a wider range of ages, genders and racial backgrounds at the wikithon, the trainee editors were helping to rebalance the scale, said Hannah Cobb, a co-founder of the event. “There’s a very specific idea of who edits Wikipedia … that doesn’t tend to be the demographic of who shows up,” she said. “There’s a really broad interest in Wikipedia in general. Everyone remembers that at school you were taught not to trust it because anyone could write it.”

blocks.caption: The experience of editing a Wikipedia page can be ‘quite empowering’, said Hannah Cobb, a co-founder of the event.  Photograph: Lily Renshaw/The Guardian

blocks.text: Previous arms industry wikithons organised by Cameron and Cobb in Manchester and London have drawn in more than 60 would-be Wikipedians at a time, including activists, journalists, Quaker members – and even Cameron’s own mother.
after newsletter promotion

Newcomers to the group were interested in how Wikipedia could be used to broaden public knowledge of confusing geopolitics, said Cobb. “There is a sense of powerlessness when it comes to countering the narrative by big tech, by governments, by the military industrial complex at large,” she said.

But for the arms industry page editors, those feelings can disappear over a few hours: “When you write something on Wikipedia, it appears immediately on the internet. I think that experience alone is quite empowering for people.”

Cobb spoke of a sense of wonder “when people realise how easy it is to actually contribute”, but attenders have a respect for Wikipedia’s commitment to rigour and quality control. And though dedicated to accuracy, the group prefers to not advertise the details of its edits over concerns that the work could be undone by other editors in bad faith.

Cameron said it was unclear if Wikipedia’s wider editorial culture would take offence over how the event was run. While wikithons are not new, the blurry line between activism and accurate dissemination of information stress-tests the platform’s rules.

blocks.caption: Another wikithon session will be held later this winter.  Photograph: Lily Renshaw/The Guardian

blocks.text: Real-world politics often spill on to Wikipedia, and editors often disagree publicly about changes. The site has also been covertly used as an informational battleground. The seasoned editor Ksenia Coffman made extensive edits to remove what she found to be flattering and sympathetic entries about Nazi party officials across Wikipedia, and in 2021, the Croatian-language version of Wikipedia was found to have been commandeered by nationalist, far-right organisers who made ideologically motivated edits.

Cameron hopes that the regular meetings can be formalised into a WikiProject, when organised groups of editors collaborate to improve certain topic pages. She hoped her group could be adopted by WikiProject Military history, which she called “far and away the most active project on Wikipedia by miles. It’s amazingly well run.”

The London wikithon is to continue for another session in the winter, and Cameron and Cobb’s faith in encyclopedia editing as a political tool is steadfast. As Cameron said: “Wikipedia is fundamentally anti-fascist.”

articles.title: Streeting delays defence jobs plan for young people after union pushback
articles.summary:
UK defence secretary had been due to unveil proposals on Thursday until concerns were raised at 11th hour

Wes Streeting has been forced to delay the publication of a plan to get more young…

blocks.text: Wes Streeting has been forced to delay the publication of a plan to get more young people into defence industry jobs after pushback from trade unions, the Guardian understands.

The defence secretary had been due to announce the proposals on Thursday, but some unions in the sector are understood to have reacted angrily to the plans, accusing the government of bypassing their members and minimising their roles in job creation.

The delay risks derailing a planned series of government announcements to tackle the youth jobs crisis, with ministers stating on Monday that jobs plans in business services, construction, technology and defence would be published this week.

Streeting is expected to visit Telford on Thursday to unveil a major new gun production facility run by German defence giant Rheinmetall, after promising that the defence jobs plan would “help deliver thousands of opportunities for young people, including an increase in the number of people supported through apprenticeship programmes in the defence sector to at least 14,000 annually by 2035”.

But the Guardian understands that unions representing workers in the sector were shown the plan just before publication, and told ministers that they would not support it, forcing the 11th-hour delay.

Sources at the Ministry of Defence (MoD) confirmed the delay, but played down the role of unions in the hold-up, stating there were issues that still had to be worked through, but that it would be published “in due course”.

Union leaders are understood to have told ministers that the plan was weak and did not acknowledge the role of unions in promoting “build British” defence policies and the creation of jobs for young people, especially apprentices. Further meetings between the ministers and union representatives are “imminent”, said one source.

“Wes Streeting has to recognise that unions have a vital role to play in developing good jobs in the defence industry, but this plan lacked a union voice and the voice of workers who are meant to be at the heart of it,” said a union source. “Any union representing people in this industry can see that this plan doesn’t do the job, and they will have to go back to the drawing board.”

A MoD source said that the department had a positive relationship with the affected unions, and downplayed reports of a rift. “This department is looking to create thousands of jobs in defence and a comprehensive plan will be published in due course.”

A spokesperson for the MoD said: “The defence jobs plan continues to be developed and will be published when ready. We work closely with trade unions and are committed to our mission to create thousands of well-paid, unionised defence jobs in every part of the country.”

The delay will come as a blow for Streeting, who last month said he was overseeing a “ministry for growth”, adding that he was determined the defence industry should play its part in tackling what he called the “moral emergency” of almost 1 million 16- to 24-year-olds not in education, employment or training (Neet).
Labour, which is coming under increasing pressure to increase defence spending to 3% of GDP, has been keen to demonstrate that the rapid increase in spending will result in jobs in the UK.

Last month defence contractors promised to create 40,000 apprenticeships, work experience placements and jobs for young people each year. “I think we have a responsibility, as we’re investing more in the defence of the realm, to do so in a way that boosts British jobs, British industry, and helps to deal with this moral emergency,” said Streeting at the time. “I want the Ministry of Defence to be a ministry of growth and a ministry of opportunity, and that’s how we’re going to direct our defence spending.”
The defence jobs plan was due to be published before the publication of former Labour cabinet minister Alan Milburn’s final report on Neets, which is now expected next month after a delay.

Reacting to the pledge made by defence industry players last month, Milburn said the industry had shown “what is possible when employers step up,” adding: “Defence is one of our great industries – it has both the scale and the opportunity to give young people the experience, skills and confidence they need to build a career.”

articles.title: Mystery of Roman sarcophagus unearthed at Westminster Abbey solved at last, expert says
articles.summary:
Archaeologist says skeleton inside coffin inscribed to Valerius Amandinus is likely to be remains of 11th-century abbot

It has all the ingredients of a chilling mystery: the skeleton of an…

blocks.text: It has all the ingredients of a chilling mystery: the skeleton of an unknown man discovered within a Roman sarcophagus unearthed in the grounds of Westminster Abbey.
Now an expert has said he has solved the longstanding “who-is-it”, suggesting the remains belonged to a medieval abbot.

First discovered in 1820, the limestone sarcophagus was officially excavated in 1869 from what is now an area of grass along the north side of the nave, but was once the yard of a sacristy built by Henry III. But the discovery spawned a mystery: whose remains were inside?

While the sarcophagus itself was from the late Roman period, with a Latin inscription to one Valerius Amandinus and Roman decoration on one side, no Roman artefacts were found in subsequent excavations of the area.

“That was not its original place of burial,” said Prof Warwick Rodwell, a consultant archaeologist at Westminster Abbey, noting it was likely the sarcophagus was originally housed in the wall recess of a mausoleum, and that Valerius Amandinus was a wealthy individual.

What’s more, the lid of the fourth-century sarcophagus was decorated with a large, carved cross that was later shown to be a modification of the original lid. “It runs the full length and the width of the lid, and it’s a very specific late Anglo-Saxon cross type,” Rodwell said.

Writing in the Journal of the British Archaeological Association, Rodwell not only describes what was previously known about the sarcophagus but sets out the findings of a more recent investigation in 2018 as part of plans to display the sarcophagus in the Queen’s Diamond Jubilee Galleries.
As part of that work the sarcophagus was taken to a laboratory and its lid removed. “And there, inside it, was the skeleton,” Rodwell said.

The discovery was something of a surprise given written records had suggested the skeleton had been lost. However, Rodwell said the bones tallied with those depicted in 19th-century drawings. A subsequent analysis suggested the remains belonged to a man who was 5ft 9in tall and aged between 35 and 49.

In another twist, when the inside of the sarcophagus was cleaned, experts found a rectangular outline in a white substance in the bottom of the sarcophagus. Rodwell said this suggests the body had been covered in powdered lime before being placed into a wooden coffin that sat inside the sarcophagus.

Crucially, radiocarbon dating of the bones suggested they were from the late 10th or early 11th century. Now Rodwell said he had the answer to the identity of the dead man, suggesting it was most likely a medieval abbott.
“Nobody of lower rank would have been buried in anything like that,” he said, adding that the lid was another clue. “The Latin cross again points to a major ecclesiastic.”

According to Rodwell, there are two possible abbots who fit the bill: Ælfwig, who died in about 1020, and Wulfnoth who died in about 1049. Rodwell believes Ælfwig is the most likely candidate, noting he was already a monk at Westminster when the previous abbot died, and spent about 27 years in the role.

Rodwell suggested the re-used sarcophagus was most likely interred in the eastern arm of the abbey church, with the lid as a floor slab, before being dug up and reburied during the construction work of Henry III.
“It’s like so much in archaeology,” said Rodwell. “There’s a lot more complication than one initially sees.”

articles.title: Troubled waters: life during wartime for Iranians on the strait of Hormuz
articles.summary:
Despite US-Israeli airstrikes and Tehran’s attacks on shipping, the waterway still has to provide a lifeline for those that live and work there

Capt Farouq turns the wheel as he watches the…
articles.byline: Stefanie Glinski ; photographs by Mohammad Mohsenifar in Bandar Abbas/on Hormuz Island

blocks.text: Capt Farouq turns the wheel as he watches the ferry terminal of Bandar Abbas grow smaller, its bright lights flickering in the distance.

In front of him, the navigation radar beeps periodically, its green and pink lights glowing in the darkness. The ferry, today at about half capacity with roughly 100 passengers, turns and heads into the darkness of the strait of Hormuz.

blocks.caption: Capt Farouq pulls into the deeper waters

items: Capt Farouq pulls into the deeper waters

blocks.caption: He’s been a captain for the past 18 years, and the strait of Hormuz is his second home

items: He’s been a captain for the past 18 years, and the strait of Hormuz is his second home

blocks.text: Farouq, 39, sits comfortably in his cabin, overlooking the pitch black horizon as he sails towards Hormuz Island, a short commute of about half an hour from the Iranian mainland’s Haqqani Port, for 340,000 toman, about £1. He is relaxed and smiles as he pulls into the deeper waters. He’s been a captain for the past 18 years, and the strait of Hormuz is his second home.

Farouq says the crossings have not stopped since the start of the US-Israeli war on Iran on 28 February, although passenger numbers are down and the journey has become more dangerous. For months, Farouq has heard explosions coming from the strait, unclear as to whether that is air defence or attacks, or both. Tonight is no different.

Inside the ferry, passengers say they have gotten used to the sounds too, and, to an extent, the war itself. They drink tea and smoke cigarettes. Some nap, while others entertain their children. It’s hot and humid, the air thick, the windows fogged with condensation.

blocks.caption: One of the ships stranded in the strait of Hormuz

items: One of the ships stranded in the strait of Hormuz

blocks.text: Even with a fragile ceasefire in place, here on the coast, it has barely felt as though the war has stopped.

According to Iranian government sources, attacks on the southern port of Bandar Abbas have damaged 760 fishing and commercial vessels. Farouq says his own ferry was also damaged by shrapnel while docked at the port, though it was quickly repaired.

Since the start of the war, Iranian forces have repeatedly attacked vessels attempting to cross the strait. In the first week of October alone, at least 12 attacks were reported against oil, liquefied natural gas and liquefied petroleum gas tankers, sending oil prices back above $100 a barrel.
With pressure mounting on the US president, Donald Trump, before the midterm elections, he is rumoured to be once again considering strikes.
But beyond the headlines and global markets, the strait is first and foremost a lifeline for many Iranians living in the southern province of Hormozgan.

blocks.caption: Fishers returning from sea

items: Fishers returning from sea

blocks.caption: Two fishers carry a box at shoreline with small boat in background
Fishers in Bandar Abbas selling their catch on the street

items: Fishers in Bandar Abbas selling their catch on the street

blocks.text: Fishers, captains and harbour workers all depend on the strait for their livelihoods and the war has made their work increasingly difficult. Fishers can no longer venture as far out, ports have come under attack, and many people fled Bandar Abbas in the early months of the war for smaller, more remote villages in search of safety.

blocks.caption: Local residents fishing for their own daily consumption

items: Local residents fishing for their own daily consumption

blocks.caption: Man crouched down reeling in line at water’s edge

blocks.text: Anvar Sadat, a 38-year-old fisher who works at Bandar Abbas’s fish market, says business has slowed and that making ends meet has become increasingly difficult.
“Fishing boats can’t go out as freely as before the war, and our movement is restricted,” he says, adding that several of his colleagues in the city have been killed in attacks.

blocks.caption: Anvar Sadat, who works at the fish market in Bandar Abbas

items: Anvar Sadat, who works at the fish market in Bandar Abbas

blocks.text: “This place was hell,” says Abdul Salam, a 45-year-old garbage collector. The beaches, particularly those near the port, were among the most dangerous places during the height of the war, he says, describing heavy attacks that forced him to stop working almost entirely to avoid the risk.

Life on the island, however, has been different, Farouq explains as he steers into the small, dimly lit port of Hormuz Island, his last crossing of the day before heading back to his family for the night.

blocks.caption: Hassan, 28, cafe owner – has run a cafe on the island for eight years

items: Hassan, 28, cafe owner – has run a cafe on the island for eight years

blocks.caption: Two people sit playing a board game with cafe counter behind

blocks.text: Hormuz Island has long been known as a kind of “hippy paradise”, a place Iranians have come to regard as “free”. Artists and creatives moved here from bigger cities in search of peace; women swim in bathing suits, writers and painters find space to work, and life moves slower. There is “love and magic” here, as Yashar, a 35-year-old surfer, puts it, “a different rhythm”.

blocks.caption: Yashar, a 35-year-old surfer

items: Yashar, a 35-year-old surfer

blocks.caption: A group of local women swimming off the coast of Hormuz Island

items: A group of local women swimming off the coast of Hormuz Island

blocks.text: Life here has changed little, Yashar says, although the war has brought some new restrictions, and a handful of attacks, mostly on infrastructure. The roughly 8,000 residents are trying to support each other, and to preserve the sense of freedom that has set the island apart, he adds.

The government has closed off parts of Hormuz Island’s north, but beyond the now restricted areas, life has continued, he explains. “As long as you don’t go north, they leave you alone,” he says of the army.

blocks.caption: Omran, a 45-year-old tour guide – the tourism sector has been hit by the conflict

items: Omran, a 45-year-old tour guide – the tourism sector has been hit by the conflict

blocks.caption: A tour guide looks out from a shaded hut over sandy terrain toward buildings and the sea
The Majara hotel, also known as Rainbow accommodation, is one of Hormuz’s attractions. It has been closed since the beginning of the war

items: The Majara hotel, also known as Rainbow accommodation, is one of Hormuz’s attractions. It has been closed since the beginning of the war

blocks.text: “The tourism sector has taken the biggest hit,” says Omran, a 45-year-old tour guide, adding that he prefers to go by his first name only. “Guesthouses and homestays remain closed, as do restaurants and many cafes.” Visitors have largely stopped coming since the war, dealing a heavy blow to an island whose economy depends on tourism and fishing, both of which have been disrupted.

blocks.caption: The Salt valley on Hormuz Island, one of the island’s tourist attractions

items: The Salt valley on Hormuz Island, one of the island’s tourist attractions

blocks.text: From the higher parts of the island, Omran says, it is possible to see deep into the strait on clear days, when the haze lifts and the humid air clears, all the way to the mountains of Khasab in Oman.

Residents have climbed up these barren mountains of red and white stone, at times watching the war unfold in the distance. Tankers remain stranded in the strait, explosions can be heard regularly. Yet residents also say the war has not driven them from the island.

blocks.caption: One of the ships stranded in the strait of Hormuz

items: One of the ships stranded in the strait of Hormuz

blocks.text: Khaleh Kaniz, a 67-year-old painter who was born and raised on Hormuz, laughs when asked whether she had considered leaving in February, at the start of the war.

blocks.caption: Khaleh Kaniz, a 67-year-old painter

items: Khaleh Kaniz, a 67-year-old painter

blocks.text: “Why should we leave? Where would we go? Our homes and our lives are here.”

articles.title: Rising emissions and temperatures: The cost of Trump's climate retreat is now clear
articles.summary: The world is set to breach the critical 1.5-degree temperature limit, with Donald Trump's US withdrawal from climate action worsening the outlook, according to a UN report. But there is a small…

image.caption: Decades of insufficient action to cut emissions mean the world will exceed 1.5 C of warming, according to the UNImage: imageBROKER/McPHOTO/BilderBox/IMAGO

blocks.text: For over a decade, scientists have warned the world must limit global warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 Fahrenheit) to avoid the most severe consequences of climate change.
That goal is no longer within reach.

Decades of "insufficient" action on cutting the fossil fuel emissions heating the planet means overshooting 1.5-degree temperature threshold is now "imminent and unavoidable," according to the United Nations Environment Program's (UNEP) annual Emissions Gap Report.

If current climate policies continue, temperatures will rise by an average of 2.8 degrees Celsius above pre-industrial levels within this century. But even if countries meet their new climate pledges, global warming is still projected to reach 2.6 degrees Celsius. Both scenarios would tip the world into a period of catastrophic weather extremes.

The projections reflect a gap between what governments promise to do and the action they are taking to curb emissions. Some 167 countries have submitted climate action plans to the UN, covering 83% of global greenhouse gas emissions. But those pledges to cut emissions fall far short of what is needed to limit warming.

Among the world's largest emitters, Indonesia, China and the United States saw emissions rise in 2025, according to preliminary estimates. The increase in the US "far exceeded that of all other countries," driven by a resurgence of coal — the dirtiest fossil fuel source — and rising electricity demand, partly linked to massive AI data center expansion.

The outlook has worsened in part because of US President Donald Trump's withdrawal of the United States from the historic Paris climate accord in which the world came together in 2015 to agree to halt climate change. The US is the second-largest annual emitter of climate-warping greenhouse gases.
Since Trump entered the Oval Office for a second time, his administration has taken a sledgehammer to climate policy, gutting environmental regulations and expanding oil and gas production.

"The main takeaway is simple — governments need to get on with enacting policies that cut fossil fuel use as soon as possible," said Bill Hare, CEO of the global science and policy institute Climate Analytics, of the report.
What does overshooting mean for the planet?

Exceeding 1.5 degrees Celsius even temporarily sets humanity on a dangerous course, as it increases the risk of triggering potentially irreversible or difficult-to-undo "tipping points," like the loss of coral reefs, long-term retreat of ice sheets, and the Amazon Rainforest turning into a grassland.

As ecosystems disappear and sea levels rise, these changes could trigger a deadly chain reaction, releasing more greenhouse gases and accelerating warming, dramatically increasing the likelihood of deadly extreme weather.

This summer alone, Europe recorded more than 32,000 excess deaths related to heat and nearly 1,500 people died in a flash floods in Nepal and Tibet, after climate change laid the groundwork for a glacier to collapse.

blocks.caption: Residents carry their belongings salvaged from their damaged homes filled with mud and debris following a deadly glacier collapse in NepalImage: Rajesh Kumar Singh/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: But scientists maintain 1.5 degrees Celsius is not a magic number, and that every fraction of a degree of warming brings escalating risks. To reduce the risk of future damage, countries should still focus on rapidly transitioning away from fossil fuels, the largest contributor to global climate change, and toward renewable energy like solar and wind.
Now the best-case scenario is overshooting 1.5 degrees Celsius for a short time before bringing temperatures back down quickly.

"Overshoot is not surrender," UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres said in a press statement. "We can still keep it as small and as short as possible — and bring temperatures back below 1.5 degrees before the end of the century."
How can the world limit overshoot?

UNEP lays out a scenario in which the world sees warming peak at 1.7 to 1.8 degrees Celsius around mid-century, before falling back to 1.5 Celsius by 2100. Getting there would require steep emissions cuts of 69% by 2040, relative to 2025 levels.

It would also require removing 330 billion metric tons of carbon dioxide from the atmosphere and storing it in the ground. But recent studies have cast doubt on the feasibility and costs of the technology, as well as the nascent carbon removal industry's ability to scale as quickly as required to meet climate goals.
The UN warns any delays will make the challenge harder, saying that every five years that emissions remain at current levels adds about 0.1 Celsius to projected peak warming.
"We must pull out all the stops to minimize peak warming and return to 1.5 Celsius by the end of the century," Inger Andersen, Executive Director of UNEP, said in a press release. "This is possible."
Climate policy works

Still, climate policies have proven effective in reducing emissions. The UNEP report draws on more than 200 studies that analyze how measures like carbon taxes, government climate targets, building codes and subsidies for low-carbon technologies are working.

Carbon-pricing schemes have been the most widely studied so far. China's pilot schemes reduced emissions by about 11%, while the European Union's emissions trading system saw an 8% cut, compared with projected levels without these policies.
"There are more opportunities than ever to accelerate action," according to the report, pointing to the boom in renewable energy since the adoption of the Paris Agreement a decade ago.
Pakistan's solar boom shields some from energy shocks

Global renewable electricity capacity has grown three times faster than anticipated, and solar build-out grew seven times faster. In 2024, more than 90% of renewable projects were cheaper than fossil fuel alternatives.

While total energy supply from coal, oil and gas has continued to rise, that's happened at a slower rate than was projected in 2015. And coal use is likely to peak and decline by the end of the decade.

"We have a wealth of success stories showing that emissions can be cut quickly," Andersen said. "It is now up to nations to urgently put in place policies that spark fast, deep and sustained emissions reductions, and put the world on track for a more stable climate and more stable economies and societies."

articles.title: Australia’s largest datacentre operator NextDC’s shares dive as Melbourne expansion delayed
articles.summary:
NextDC has told investors that its plans to double the size of its west Melbourne datacentre has hit an obstacle in community objections to 22m high power poles

Australia’s largest…

blocks.text: Australia’s largest datacentre operator has been forced to delay the controversial expansion of its M3 site in Melbourne’s west amid a pause in construction of new 22m power poles following community protest.

On Wednesday, NextDC told the Australian Stock Exchange that delays to electricity provider Jemena’s upgrade of the power poles – essential to delivering the increased electricity required by the expanded West Footscray site – would mean the expansion would be pushed back to the 2027/2028 financial year.

The company’s share price dropped from over $9 a share down to $5.69 a share after exiting the trading halt on Wednesday. Due to the deferred billing and delivery of contracted capacity in M3, the company had reduced its net revenue guidance to between $475m and $500m from between $615m and $640m.

NextDC told the market Jemena had suspended the works due to safety concerns, lack of access to sites arising from community and stakeholder opposition, and due to the local council not approving the building of the 22 metre high power poles – up from 11 metres today, according to Jemena - while further community consultations take place.

NextDC and Jemena are looking at other options for supplying the increased electricity needs, including alternate locations for poles through industrial zones or connecting via underground power connections.
The expansion of the NextDC site is intended to take it from offering capacity of 60 megawatts today to 225MW, processing power which NextDC has already sold to customers.

The site has faced strong opposition from locals in West Footscray. Guardian Australia reported in May that residents were concerned about the scale of the expansion, the construction noise, and the potential for diesel generators being used in the event of power outages.

The total planned expansion is expected to double the size of the M3 site to 10 hectares when complete. NextDC said construction of the new data halls would continue despite the delay in grid supply from Jemena, but said the Victorian government’s planning decision on a permit for stages six and seven of the construction were taking longer than expected.

NextDC’s chief executive, Craig Scroggie, told investors in a call on Wednesday that he expects the earliest approval for the expansion would be February 2027, as the Victorian government is about to enter caretaker mode for the 28 November state election.

The application has been with the state government since February 2026, and Scroggie blamed the change of premier from Jacinta Allen to Ben Carroll and the associated cabinet reshuffle for delaying approvals.
Scroggie said it was “disappointing to be facing this particular technical challenge” for M3, but he was confident it could be approved.
after newsletter promotion

“We comply with all of the development requirements under the planning rules. And obviously acknowledging the community concerns more recently, on datacentres, generally, more community consultation is required about … the ongoing operation, development and construction issues on the site.”
Sean Brown, a West Footscray resident and Citizens of Tottenham member, said the community had not set out to reduce shareholder value in raising concerns about the project.
“Our goal was to get a fair outcome for our community and to make sure that proper safety framework is in place – and we still haven’t got those,” he said.
“We’re not stopping. This is continuing until we get a fair outcome for the residents.”
Brown said “whoever forms government” and becomes planning minister after the state election “will be definitely hearing from us”.
“It will be a pretty toxic thing to sign off on.”

articles.title: China to Ridon: Why not suggest closing the entire embassy?
articles.summary: "Why not suggest closing the entire embassy?" This was the response of the Chinese Embassy in Manila to Bicol Saro party-list Representative Terry Ridon's statement urging the Philippine government…

blocks.text: Published October 21, 2026 12:52pm
"Why not suggest closing the entire embassy?"

This was the response of the Chinese Embassy in Manila to Bicol Saro party-list Representative Terry Ridon's statement urging the Philippine government to deport lower-ranking Chinese diplomatic personnel.

Posted on Wednesday, the Chinese embassy reacted to Ridon's remarks after the Department of Foreign Affairs (DFA) summoned Chinese Ambassador Jing Quan for claiming that China would "easily win" if it resorted to force in the West Philippine Sea.

"So 'yun ang maganda pag-aralan ng DFA at ng ating Pangulo. Kung hindi po papaalsin po 'yung embahador, 'yung po ang mga lesser diplomats na lang po 'yung palayasin, particularly because nag-usap na kahapon, marami pa rin ho silang sinasabi hanggang ngayon," Ridon said in a press conference.

(That is something for the DFA and our President to consider. If the ambassador is not expelled, then the lower-ranking diplomats could be expelled instead, particularly because they already had a discussion yesterday, yet they are still making statements about it up to now.)
DFA had summoned Jing Quan to convey the Philippines' "serious concern and strong objection" to his recent remarks.

"It is not the place of a foreign mission to publicly criticize or taunt Philippine officials and legislators who are acting within their mandates. As a democracy, the Philippines values freedom of expression and a plurality of voices, and it will not accept attempts by a foreign envoy to intimidate those who exercise them," DFA said.
On Saturday, the Chinese Embassy released a statement amid talks of possibly declaring Jing persona non grata after his remarks were perceived by some lawmakers as "threats" against the Philippines.
"Some senators and house representatives are talking about declaring the Chinese ambassador persona non grata. Is this threat or coercion?" the Chinese Embassy said in a social media post.
"But anyway, just do it. Otherwise, STOP BLUFFING," it added.

In a separate social media post on Wednesday, the Chinese embassy described the statement of Senator Kiko Pangilinan as "thuggish, hooligan-style language," after the senator urged President Ferdinand "Bongbong" Marcos Jr. to send Jing back to China.

"Mr. President if you can send Duterte, Quiboloy and Romualdez to jail, declare POGO illegal and have them shutdown, assert our sovereignty against Chinese aggression then you can most certainly send this arrogant, insulting, crude and insolent alien back to his country of origin," Pangilinan said.

"Using thuggish, hooligan-style language to launch personal attacks on others—is this the calibre and standards of a Philippine senator? Is this the diplomacy and prudence that the DFA claims to uphold?" the Chinese Embassy said in response to the senator's post.
Earlier this year, Marcos rejected calls to declare Jing persona non grata amid calls from legislators to expel some Chinese embassy officials over the West Philippine Sea row.

In 2016, the Permanent Court of Arbitration in The Hague ruled in favor of the Philippines over China's claims in the South China Sea, saying that it had "no legal basis." China has refused to recognize the decision. — VDV, GMA News

articles.title: Malacañang asks SC to revisit ruling on 2024, 2025 national budgets
articles.summary: Malacañang on Wednesday said that it will ask the Supreme Court to reconsider its recent ruling declaring as unconstitutional the General Appropriations Acts (GAAs) for 2024 and 2025 due to budget…

blocks.text: Published October 21, 2026 12:42pm

Malacañang on Wednesday said that it will ask the Supreme Court to reconsider its recent ruling declaring as unconstitutional the General Appropriations Acts (GAAs) for 2024 and 2025 due to budget increases made by Congress.
Palace Press Officer Undersecretary Claire Castro announced this in a press briefing, saying that Malacañang “respectfully disagrees” with certain parts of the high court’s ruling.
She said the Office of the Solicitor General has been tasked to file the motion for reconsideration.

“Ang inilatag na kondisyon ng Korte Suprema na dapat ay malagpasan muna ang kabuuang koleksyon sa kabuuang revenue target bago magamit ang unprogrammed appropriations, sa ating pananaw ay tahasang pagbabago ng mga kondisyong itinakda ng Kongreso bilang sangay ng pamahalaan na naatasan ng ating Konstitusyon na bumalangkas ng taunang pambansang budget,” Casto said.
“Magalang nating hinihiling sa Korte Suprema na muling suriin ang kanilang desisyon,” she added.
(We respectfully ask the Supreme Court to carefully review their decision.)

The Supreme Court said the 2024 budget was voided due to P449.5-billion increase in unprogrammed appropriations, while the 2025 GAA was likewise struck down because of the additional P17.99 billion for the Special Road Fund of the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH). Both of these adjustments resulted in an increase in the president’s total recommended appropriations, the SC said.

As for the 2026 GAA, the high court deemed as unconstitutional Special Provisions 1(a) and (b), Chapter XLIII authorizing unprogrammed appropriations. It then set conditions that would allow such appropriations to be constitutional. — RSJ, GMA News

articles.title: Revilla asks Sandiganbayan for permission to file demurrer in malversation case
articles.summary: Former Senator Ramon “Bong” Revilla, Jr. and his co-accused, JP Mendoza, asked the Sandiganbayan to allow them to file a motion seeking to dismiss the P92.8 million malversation case against them in…

blocks.text: FLOOD CONTROL PROJECT
Published October 21, 2026 12:37pm

Former Senator Ramon “Bong” Revilla, Jr. and his co-accused, JP Mendoza, asked the Sandiganbayan to allow them to file a motion seeking to dismiss the P92.8 million malversation case against them in connection to anomalous flood control project in Pandi, Bulacan.
The Sandiganbayan Third Division was referring to the leave of court to file demurrer to evidence filed by Revilla and Mendoza.
A demurrer to evidence is a pleading asking the court to dismiss the charges on the ground of weak evidence.

Back in July 31, the Sandiganbayan Third Division, via a split 2-1 vote, granted Revilla’s petition for bail by citing that the prosecution failed to present an “iota of proof" showing that Revilla had either explicitly or implicitly agreed to receive an advance kickback.

“The prosecution has not yet presented any proof that connects the alleged acts of obtaining the list and of facilitating the funding of the subject project to the eventual understanding that the recovery of the advance kickbacks allegedly paid to accused Revilla will be recovered by some of the co-accused by way of malversation,” the resolution, penned by Associate Justice Fritz Bryn Anthony Delos Santos, said.
The Sandiganbayan set Revilla’s cash bond at P1 million for his temporary liberty. —VAL, GMA News

articles.title: ICC prosecutors drop one drug war killing from Rodrigo Duterte case
articles.summary: Prosecutors at the International Criminal Court have dropped one alleged killing of a high-value drug target from their case against former president Rodrigo Duterte, after judges ruled it fell…

blocks.text: October 21, 2026 | 12:35pm

Former Philippine President Rodrigo Duterte appears at the International Criminal Court (ICC) in The Hague on September 16, 2026, during a preparatory session as he faces charges over his “war on drugs,” which killed thousands.
AFP / Pool / Piroschka Van De Wouw

MANILA, Philippines — Prosecutors at the International Criminal Court have dropped one alleged killing of a high-value drug target from their case against former president Rodrigo Duterte, after judges ruled it fell outside the time frame of the charge, according to a court filing.

The killing, listed as Incident 57, was one of eight that prosecutors sought to add to the case ahead of trial. They filed it under Count 2, which covers the alleged murders of “high-value targets,” or suspected major drug figures, during Duterte’s first year as president, from July 2016 to July 2017.

In an October 9 ruling, Trial Chamber III said the killing fit the type and locations of crimes covered by Count 2 but took place outside that period. The judges said prosecutors could not stretch the defined period that they themselves established for the case.

The judges admitted the seven other new incidents, bringing the total to 56, up from 49 when the charges were confirmed in April. An incident can involve more than one victim: the original 49 cover 76 murders and two attempted murders. The court has not said publicly how many victims the seven new incidents add.

The filing, dated Wednesday, October 20 and signed by Acting Prosecutor Mame Mandiaye Niang, shows prosecutors removed Incident 57 from their trial brief, the document that lays out the case they will present in court.

Prosecutors, however, left their lists of witnesses and evidence unchanged, although the October 9 ruling had ordered those updated as well. They said material connected to the killing, combined with other evidence about it, remains relevant to “the contextual elements of crimes against humanity, and Mr Duterte’s individual criminal responsibility.” Large parts of their explanation were redacted in the public document.
A killing counts as a crime against humanity only if it was part of a widespread or systematic attack on civilians carried out under a state or organizational policy.

Besides the high-value target killings, the charges cover alleged killings in Davao City while Duterte was mayor, from 2013 to around June 2016. They also cover alleged murders and attempted murders during barangay clearance operations from July 2016 to September 2018.
The trial of the former president opens November 30.

Super typhoon Rosal as of 10:40 a.m. on Oct. 21, 2026.

MANILA, Philippines — Batanes has been placed under Tropical Cyclone Wind Signal No. 2 as Super Typhoon Rosal (international name: Champi) maintained its strength while moving west-northwestward over the sea east of Northern Luzon, state weather bureau PAGASA said.
In its 11 a.m. bulletin, PAGASA said the center of Rosal's eye was 845 kilometers east of Northern Luzon as of 10 a.m.
The super typhoon is currently at its peak intensity, packing maximum sustained winds of 215 kilometers per hour (kph) near the center and gusts of up to 265 kph, with a central pressure of 900 hPa.
Rosal is moving west-northwestward at 25 kph while its winds extend outward up to 780 kilometers from its center.
PAGASA raised Tropical Cyclone Wind Signal No. 2 over Batanes, warning residents of possible gale-force winds of 62 to 88 kph within 24 hours that pose minor to moderate threats to life and property.
Meanwhile, Tropical Cyclone Wind Signal No. 1 remains in effect over the following areas in Luzon, where strong winds (39 to 61 kph) are expected within 36 hours:
