articles.title: Blood clots have halted Jalen Hurts's NFL season. They've also been a problem for other sports stars
articles.summary: Football player Jalen Hurts of the Philadelphia Eagles is expected to miss the rest of the season due to blood clots in his lungs. The announcement brings new attention to the condition and raises…

image.caption: Jalen Hurts of the Philaelphia Eagles plays against the Los Angeles Rams at Lincoln Financial Field in Philadelphia earlier this month. He's expected to miss the rest of the season because of blood clots in his lungs, a person familiar with the situation told The Associated Press on Monday. (Emilee

blocks.text: Health

Football player Jalen Hurts of the Philadelphia Eagles is expected to miss the rest of the season due to blood clots in his lungs. The announcement brings new attention to the condition and raises questions about why so many high-profile athletes have been diagnosed with blood clots in recent years.
Questions remain about why so many athletes have been diagnosed with blood clots in recent years
Jalen Hurts of the Philadelphia Eagles is the latest professional athlete to endure blood clots, joining NBA players Victor Wembanyama, Chris Bosh, Damian Lillard and others.

The one-time Super Bowl MVP is expected to miss the rest of the season because of blood clots in his lungs, a person familiar with the situation told The Associated Press on Monday. The person spoke to the AP on condition of anonymity because of the sensitivity of the health matter.

Hurts was placed on injured reserve Saturday, two days after the team revealed he has a blood clot in his calf. The Eagles and Hurts' agent, Nicole Lynn, released more information on his condition Monday. They said Hurts has deep vein thrombosis and bilateral pulmonary emboli, meaning a blood clot has travelled to the lungs.
The diagnosis brought new attention to the condition, its risks and treatments, while raising questions about why so many athletes have been diagnosed with blood clots in recent years.
What is deep vein thrombosis?

Deep vein thrombosis, or DVT, is the term for a blood clot that forms in a deep vein, usually in the lower legs. Sometimes, these clots can break off and travel into the lungs, lodging in a blood vessel to block blood flow. That's called a pulmonary embolism and it can be life-threatening.
Any number of things can cause deep vein thrombosis, ranging from immobility and trauma to family history and dehydration.

Symptoms include inexplicable swelling and discoloration or pain, or some combination of those factors, and experts say the worry is the clot travelling through the bloodstream, causing a pulmonary embolism or death.

"When you have a DVT in the leg or the arm, there's a chance that it will break free, and when it breaks free, it can end up lodged in the lung," Mary Cushman, a hematologist and professor of medicine at the University of Vermont, told the AP previously. "And if it's large enough, that can kill a person."
What is the treatment?
Taking blood thinners is the most common course of action when it comes to treatment.
Sometimes surgery is involved, or blood thinners are used for the long term.
The treatment Hurts is using involves blood thinners, and he will not be allowed to participate in any football activities until he is off them.
Are athletes more likely to have it?

Richard Ricciardi, a professor at the George Washington University School of Nursing, says there is no evidence to suggest elite athletes are more predisposed to blood clots than people of comparable ages in the general population.

NHL goalie Frederik Andersen minds the net for the Carolina Hurricanes during the playoffs last season. A few years ago, he had medical tests that found blood clots. (Matt Slocum/The Associated Press)
"I do not believe there are any large-scale studies that compare elite athletes with non-athletes," Ricciardi said.
"Athletes are generally considered low risk for blood clots, but they face a cluster of sport-specific risk factors, so they may have a higher risk than expected for young, fit people.

"High-contact sports theoretically could raise blood clot risk, primarily through collision and trauma-induced blood vessel wall injury," he said. "But to my knowledge no studies directly quantify how much contact sports increase risk versus noncontact sports."
The risk of people in their 20s and 30s developing deep vein thrombosis or a pulmonary embolism is one in 10,000.
Can air travel increase risks?
"Frequent long-haul air travel plausibly increases blood clot risk in elite athletes, but to my knowledge no athlete-specific studies have been conducted," Ricciardi said.
"Risk is greatest in flights of eight hours or more. However, the risk per flight remains low in healthy, fit individuals, and risk is concentrated in those with additional health risk factors."

The U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)'s website says blood clots can form in deep veins of the legs during travel because people are sitting still in a confined space for long periods of time.

It says "most people who develop travel-associated blood clots" have additional risks for blood clots, including prior blood clots, an inherited blood clotting disorder or a family history of blood clots.
San Antonio Spurs forward Victor Wembanyama plays in a pre-season game against the Phoenix Suns earlier this month. (Ross D. Franklin/The Associated Press)
Other athletes with blood clots

Victor Wembanyama: His 2024-25 season ended after he was diagnosed with a blood clot in his right shoulder. The seven-foot-four phenom from France bounced back last season, when he finished third in NBA MVP voting and won the league's Defensive Player of the Year award as he led the San Antonio Spurs to the NBA Finals.

Damian Lillard: The nine-time NBA All-Star scored 16 points with the Milwaukee Bucks on March 18, 2025, and about a week later, the team said he had deep vein thrombosis in his right calf. Lillard returned for the playoffs and tore his Achilles tendon, an injury that kept him out of the lineup last season in his return to Portland.
Blood clots ended the basketball career of Chris Bosh, who played for the Toronto Raptors and the Miami Heat during his Hall of Fame career. (Steve Marcus/Getty Images)

Chris Bosh: A decade earlier, blood clots ended the career of the Basketball Hall of Famer. He was averaging 19.1 points and 7.4 rebounds in 33.5 minutes during the 2015-16 season and had just arrived in Toronto for that year's All-Star Game when a clot in one of his legs was discovered at the age of 31.

Ausar Thompson: The NBA All-Defensive team player missed the last month of his rookie season two years ago with a blood clot. He was not cleared to play during the first month of his second season while he worked through a medical process with the NBA and the players' union.
American golfer Nelly Korda plays a tee shot during a practice round for the Solheim Cup last month. (Alastair Grant/The Associated Press)
Nelly Korda: The current No. 1 player in women's golf missed four months in 2022 — the year after she won her first major title — because of a blood clot in her left arm that required surgery.

Frederik Andersen: Nearly three years ago, the Carolina Hurricanes goaltender had medical tests that found blood clots. He played for the Hurricanes last season when they won the Stanley Cup and is currently recovering from a knee injury with the Edmonton Oilers.
Merrill Kelly: The right-handed pitcher, has bounced back from his bouts of blood clots to play for the Arizona Diamondbacks, going 10-14 in 29 starts last season.

Christian Barmore: The New England Patriots defensive tackle was limited to four games during the 2024 season after he had blood clots. He started 15 games last season and has played in five this year with the Patriots. "I could have lost my life," Barmore said.

articles.title: AfD's Alice Weidel to unveil plan to cut EU powers — report
articles.summary: The far-right AfD will propose slashing powers of the European Union when it presents its policy paper on Wednesday, Politico reports.

image.caption: The AfD was founded in 2013 as a Euroskeptic party opposed to euro bailouts and European integration (PHOTO: Alice Weidel, 2026)Image: Fabian Weiss/ZDF/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Alice Weidel, the co-leader of Germany's far-right AfD, is expected to present her party's policy for the EU at the European Parliament on Wednesday.
According to a report from news outlet Politico, the AfD policy paper on the EU does not seek to exit the bloc or the eurozone at first.
The party rather wants to downsize the EU's powers and budget.
What's in the AfD policy paper?
Instead of direct European Parliament elections, the AfD would like to see delegates appointed by national parliaments.
The AfD would also limit the scope of the European Commission to purely administrative tasks and supplant the European Court of Justice with an arbitration tribunal.
The AfD would threaten to slash Germany's contributions to the EU budget.

Germany under the AfD would seek exemptions from EU regulations regarding issues such as migration and social policy. The AfD may also seek opt-outs of other areas such as agriculture and financial policies.
If the EU would not bend to the AfD's demands for reform, the party would then seek a German referendum on EU membership.

A referendum would be unrealistic, as it would require a constitutional amendment to the German Basic Law to take place. An amendment would require a two-thirds majority vote in both the Bundestag and upper house Bundesrat — an extremely high threshold to meet.
AfD eyes victory in next federal elections in 2029
The AfD hopes that it can implement its EU policies in 2029, when the next German and European elections will take place.

Recent German federal election surveys show the AfD in first place but it would have to form a coalition with another partner to establish a ruling majority government. That's difficult when other parties such as the conservative Christian Democratic Union refuse to have any cooperation with the AfD as part of a "firewall" policy.

articles.title: Alberta's decisive decision to stay in Canada gives Carney backing to take on Trump
articles.summary: The overwhelming vote by Alberta to stay in Canada gives Mark Carney political capital to focus on remaking the country's economy, writes the BBC's Lyse Doucet.

blocks.text: "Vote like Canada depends on it," Prime Minister Mark Carney declared to cheering crowds in Calgary last week on a stage emblazoned with bright red and white "Forever Canadian" banners.
It's a message that appears to have struck a chord with the electorate, as preliminary results show more than two-thirds of Alberta voters said they want to remain a part of Canada.
But the future of the federation does still rest on its richest province.

Alberta, with most of Canada's proven oil reserves and abundant gas and mineral wealth, is playing a pivotal role in Ottawa's drive to survive a punishing trade war with the US by diversifying trade, strengthening its economy, and forging new alliances on the other side of the world.
Carney, the former central banker who grew up in Alberta, is now Canada's builder-in-chief – at home, and beyond its borders.

Note the emphasis in his first statement after Monday's vote on separation in the province, as soon as the scale of the victory was clear: "They chose unity, to build together, and to take care of each other."
Albertans' overwhelming "yes" to stay in Canada gives him political bricks and mortar, too.
"Don't mess with Canada," warned Thomas Lukaszuk, a former lawmaker whose Forever Canadian campaign played a key role in this referendum's outcome.

Addressing elated supporters in Edmonton, the provincial capital, as the "yes" count for Canada kept tumbling in, Lukaszuk underlined that this vote "will send a very strong message to the rest of the world".
Everyone knows he's talking about the troublesome neighbour to the south – in particular its president, who keeps threatening to turn Canada into the 51st US state.
The same day Albertans were voting on their future in Canada, Trump sent his own signal north at a rally in Kansas ahead of next month's US midterm polls.
"I will let you keep ice hockey, and I will let you keep your 'O Canada' national anthem," he promised before adding: "We're only kidding."
For Canadians, it's no laughing matter.

In the run up to this referendum, Carney reiterated a warning he's often sounded that "there are some outside our borders who are working to break us, so they own us" – even if he didn't spell out who "they" is.
He didn't have to.

And, in this defining time for the separatist camp, some in their ranks didn't hide their direction of travel. Some of their most prominent leaders admitted they travelled to Washington three times last year to meet US State Department officials and outline what an independent Alberta could offer – including a possible oil pipeline through the US to the Pacific.
But the rest of the world may take only passing notice of what was, for Canada, an historic vote sparking conversations and concerns across the country, from coast to coast to coast.

"Short of a vote to separate, most foreign governments, with the exception of the United States, have little interest in domestic Canadian politics," says Professor Janice Stein, founding director of the Munk School of Global Affairs and Public Policy at the University of Toronto.

"Foreign investors are focused on the time it will take to complete major infrastructure projects, a return on investment, and predictable regulations," she explains in a nod to Carney's long list of megaprojects he hopes will eventually turbocharge economic growth. They're all costly; many will take years to build.

An ambitious blueprint already includes a proposed pipeline to the Pacific coast which opens opportunities for Alberta's oil to reach Asian markets – a move which also addresses Alberta's long-standing grievance that its economy has been stifled by federal policies, including environmental regulations.
At a rally in Alberta last week, it was Carney's comment that the pipeline "will reduce our dependence on the United States" that triggered the loudest and longest applause of the night.

After Monday's vote, Carney – the former UN Special Envoy for Climate Action and Finance – pointed to "unleashing our full potential as a global energy superpower with Alberta as its core". Political and economic pressures now seem to eclipse his green credentials.
"Build Canada Strong" has been Carney's mantra ever since he first entered politics, a complete neophyte, at the start of last year.

At home there are possible wide-reaching repercussions from the final tallies in the referendum's nine other questions which dealt with issues ranging from greater provincial powers, the costs of immigration, and potential constitutional changes.
Those results are certain to provoke debate, and deal making or breaking, involving Canada's nine other provinces and three territories. They all have their own grievances, too.

The prime minister has had to defend himself when journalists ask if he is spending too much time on foreign trips with his charm offensive to build new political alliances and trade partnerships, including an unprecedented and still uncertain offer of associate membership of the European Union.

"I can do both and I need to do both," he recently replied with his signature bluntness before listing the more than 16 bills which went through Parliament in the last session dealing with everything from major tax changes, public safety, and the price of fuel.

For now, Carney is riding high in the polls at home – including in Alberta, which doesn't traditionally support his Liberal party - in a long "political honeymoon" other beleaguered politicians would envy.

And the plain-speaking politician's strong and steady response to Trump threats, including retaliatory tariffs, has seen his star rising on the world stage. It's an unexpected turn for a country which has often been missing from top tables and has sometimes even been dismissed as "boring".
The Economist magazine decided to put Carney on their cover, on this week of weeks for Canada, with a perfect red maple leaf between his teeth.
"Mark Carney shows middle powers how to handle a dangerous world," reads one of its headlines, with an article which also focuses on Canada's "vulnerabilities" including Alberta's ballot.
"The broader takeaway from this vote might be that Canadian unity is in fine shape," remarks David Moscrop, political scientist and author of the forthcoming book On Nationalism.
"But what happens after Donald Trump is gone and Canada no longer has a single, bombastic target which drives Canadians to rally around the flag?" he asks.

Carney's decision to recently walk away from trade talks with the US gave rise to another swell of Canadian pride and patriotism. But if this trade war drags on with a country which traditionally takes 70% of Canada's exports, Canadians will feel even greater pain in their daily lives.
But today is a day to vigorously wave the maple leaf flag.
"It's a win for Team Canada and its resilience," commented CBC journalist Janyce McGregor during the public broadcaster's rolling coverage of a vast country of never-ending building issues.

articles.title: First Nations leaders praise high Alberta referendum turnout despite ballot box barriers
articles.summary: First Nations leaders believe record voter turnout in their communities helped deliver a decisive victory for treaty rights — and Canada — in Alberta's separation referendum this week, despite…

image.caption: Voters leave a polling station after casting their votes in the Alberta referendum in Calgary, Monday, Oct. 19, 2026. (The Canadian Press/Jeff McIntosh)

blocks.text: Indigenous

First Nations leaders believe record voter turnout in their communities helped deliver a decisive victory for treaty rights — and Canada — in Alberta's separation referendum this week, despite reports of some communities facing barriers at the ballot box.
Leaders urge Canada to address First Nations' concerns in wake of referendum
· CBC News
· Posted: Oct 20, 2026 5:30 PM EDT | Last Updated: 3 hours ago
Jay Telegdi, Treaty 8 campaign manager, said he spent all night Monday answering calls from First Nations people who said they were turned away from voting.

"We received many calls of polling stations opening up late, at least three that I can think of on reserve, but also polling stations running out of ballots early," Telegdi said, describing himself as sleepless and raw-voiced.

There were also reports of people being denied ballots over identification issues. Elections Alberta requires two pieces of ID if a voter's government-issued photo ID doesn't have a current physical address. On-reserve, a driver's licence might list a P.O. Box, requiring a second piece of ID in some situations.
"This was a systemic issue. Across the board, I heard it in every corner of the province, and I guarantee you lots of people were turned away and denied a right to vote because of it," he said.
Siksika Nation chief seeks 'formal explanation' after ballot shortages

In an emailed response to CBC News, Elections Alberta said the ballot shortages indicated higher-than-expected turnout among First Nations communities, with several receiving multiple ballot deliveries.

"This is a good news story, showing higher voter engagement in these locations," the agency said, adding that unofficially more communities participated than in the past — 36 in 2026 versus 33 in 2023.
Based on the calls he received, Telegdi said he believes the referendum saw the highest Indigenous voter turnout in Alberta history.
"Canada owes a deep debt of gratitude to the First Nations and Prime Minister Carney needs to recognize that," Telegdi said.
He praised First Nations chiefs for being the only people in Alberta who "stuck their neck out to challenge this referendum in court."

Chief Sheldon Sunshine of Sturgeon Lake Cree Nation was one of those people. He said the results — roughly 75 per cent of electors voted to remain while some 25 per cent voted to pursue a legally binding separation referendum — were "what we expected."
He said preliminary reports indicate "a record turnout" for his community.
"We're happy with the results, but at the end of the day it really doesn't change much," Sunshine said.
"We're still going to be dealing with a government that's been adverse to First Nations for several years."
Sturgeon Lake Cree Nation Chief Sheldon Sunshine says the whole country likely recognizes the importance of treaty now more than before the referendum began. (Eagle Andersen/CBC)

"I hope it's the end of the UCP government. The way I see it, like, I'm embarrassed for them. They initiated this whole process. They wasted a significant amount of money when we're dealing with significant challenges."
Sunshine noted "the fight is still not over," citing the Carney government's efforts to streamline pipeline development in the province.

items: Fort Chipewyan leaders criticize Elections Alberta over advance voting delays for referendum
First Nations in Alberta work to mobilize voters, prepare community members for referendum

blocks.text: A former national chief of the Assembly of First Nations (AFN) is urging Canada to deal fairly with First Nations' concerns and grievances in the wake of the referendum.
"Albertans have made their voices heard. Now, the question is: What will Ottawa do?" said Matthew Coon Come in a statement provided to CBC News on Tuesday.

Coon Come led the AFN, which advocates for First Nations countrywide, between 2000 and 2003 but before that led the Grand Council of the Crees in Quebec for two decades, including during the province's 1995 separation referendum.
First Nations prepare to Rock the Vote in referendum
Chiefs in Alberta and Quebec have been building alliances, sharing knowledge and looking to learn from people like Coon Come as they face separatist movements in both provinces.

"It is incumbent upon Canada to address the underlying issues that fuel division, including longstanding grievances, resource jurisdiction, economic fairness, and the unresolved obligations owed to First Nations," Coon Come said in the statement.
"Ignoring these issues will only deepen the divisions within our country."

AFN's current national chief, Cindy Woodhouse Nepinak, also praised the outcome in a statement on Tuesday, thanking chiefs for their work to reject "a divisive proposal that would bring needless upheaval, conflict and uncertainty for everyone."
The chiefs are now turning their attention to an upcoming First Nations-First Ministers Meeting scheduled for Oct. 26 in Ottawa where they can make their voices heard directly.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Brett Forester is a senior reporter with CBC Indigenous in Ottawa. He is a member of the Chippewas of Kettle and Stony Point First Nation in southern Ontario who previously worked as a journalist with the Aboriginal Peoples Television Network.

articles.title: Italy to deploy 500 troops to Milan after days of protests and looting
articles.summary: Government planning tougher security measures as France also says military forces will be deployed
articles.byline: Angela Giuffrida in Rome and Jon Henley in Paris

blocks.text: Italy’s government is sending 500 soldiers to Milan and vowed a “firm response from the state” after protests against the cost of living descended into clashes with police, vandalism and looting. Further demonstrations are planned on Saturday.

The government of the far-right prime minister, Giorgia Meloni, is also planning to swiftly approve tougher new security measures, including extending preventive detention for minors, cracking down on youth gangs and banning gatherings for people deemed a threat to public order, Italian media reported on Tuesday.

In France, the interior minister, Laurent Nuñez, said on Tuesday some military forces would be deployed during ⁠protests ​planned for this Saturday, “mostly to free police and gendarmes in their mission to maintain order”.

The French prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, told parliament that the police presence during Saturday’s demonstrations ⁠would be “massive” and that ​his ​goal was ​for an “immediate return ​to order” ‌after last weekend’s violent riots.

Police in Milan, in northern Italy, detained 271 young people after hooded youths set bins ablaze, ransacked shops and smashed windows, including in the area surrounding the city’s cathedral, during the unrest on Saturday and Sunday.

Police used teargas and water cannon to disperse the violent groups, who were on the fringes of an initially peaceful protest. Of those detained, 32 have been arrested, including 23 minors and 13 foreign nationals, police said on Monday. A further 28 people were reported to judicial authorities.

blocks.caption: In Milan’s Galleria Vittorio Emanuele II, brands including Chanel, Tiffany ‌and Dior have removed merchandise from ‌their windows as a precaution. Photograph: Stefano Porta/LaPresse/Shutterstock

blocks.text: Images of Saturday’s clashes in France, including mobs looting shops and public buildings set on fire, prompted several countries including the US, China and Germany to issue travel advice for their citizens. Nearly 2,400 people were arrested in one of France’s most violent recent bouts of unrest.

French authorities on Monday announced partial curfews in several cities, including Paris, Bordeaux, Lille and Nice, and after a night of relative calm, Lecornu said on Tuesday that new curfews would be imposed where they were needed.

Authorities in Paris renewed Monday night’s curfew, which would apply from 11pm on Tuesday until 6am on Wednesday to the Place de la République, where many of the weekend clashes took place, and in the central Les Halles shopping district.

Paris police ordered a temporary ban on people carrying cans or bottles of petrol or gas, and banned masks and helmets in some areas. A man was also arrested in connection with the burning down of the historic town hall in Limoges.

The Italian press agency Ansa reported that one of the security measures being considered in the country was aimed at second-generation immigrant youths, known as maranza – a slang term used to describe gangs of young people, usually from marginalised areas.
Many luxury stores in Milan’s fashion district have stayed closed amid fears of further unrest. Brands including Chanel, Tiffany ‌and Dior removed merchandise from ‌their windows as a precaution.
Other stores ransacked included the sports retailers Decathlon and Arc’teryx and the mobile phone operator Vodafone, footage showed.

“The government will respond firmly to these attacks on the state, ​including through measures aimed at curbing violence by minors,” the foreign minister, Antonio Tajani, who also serves as deputy prime minister, said after Meloni chaired a meeting with top security officials on Monday.

Meloni’s coalition, which is facing a general election next year, is reportedly planning tougher penalties for road blockades after days of protests in southern Italy by lorry drivers over fuel prices.
after newsletter promotion

Meanwhile, Milan is bracing for further protests on Saturday after a new movement, called 17 October, emerged on social media. It said it would organise demonstrations there and in other Italian cities each Saturday afternoon “until this government of thieves collapses”.
“You are the violent ones,” the group said. “You, who denied us a future. Now, we are claiming that future ourselves.”

Opposition politicians often accuse the government of using security as a propaganda tool, arguing that Italy’s leaders do little to address core issues such as education, housing and living conditions in marginalised areas.

There were also tensions during protests at the weekend over the high cost of living in other northern Italian cities, ​including Bologna, Brescia, Bergamo ​and Turin, where 28 protesters were arrested, police said.
Thousands also rallied in Lisbon and other Portuguese cities on Tuesday evening, hours after police dismantled housing protest camps at dawn and arrested 55 people.
Demonstrators in Portugal are protesting soaring housing costs, seeking to align themselves with similar actions in neighbouring Spain, where tents have been set up in central Madrid for weeks.
In Lisbon, thousands of people gathered in the central Rossio square, where protesters voted by a show of hands to re-establish their tent camp from Wednesday.
“They forced me on to the streets to shout”, read one placard. Another declared: “Lisbon is not for sale”.

articles.title: CRA awards $12M contract to subsidiary of U.S. company over non-profit Commissionaires
articles.summary: The secretary of state in charge of the Canada Revenue Agency is defending the CRA's decision to award a $12-million security contract to a Canadian subsidiary of an American multinational company…

image.caption: Wayne Long, secretary of state for the Canada Revenue Agency and financial institutions, rises during question period in the House of Commons in Ottawa on Tuesday. Long is defending the CRA's decision to award a $12-million security contract to a Canadian subsidiary of an American multinational comp

blocks.text: Politics·New

The secretary of state in charge of the Canada Revenue Agency is defending the CRA's decision to award a $12-million security contract to a Canadian subsidiary of an American multinational company over the Commissionaires.
The difference between the two bids was less than one per cent of its value, says Commissionaires spokesperson
Founded in 1925, Commissionaires is a private, not-for-profit security organization that was founded to provide meaningful employment to veterans of the Canadian Armed Forces and police services.

Publicly available documents show that in June 2026, the CRA awarded the contract to Universal Protection Service of Canada Corporation, a subsidiary of Allied Universal Security Services — a security company with ties to the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) deportation program.
It comes months after Commissionaires said the federal government told them they will no longer have first right of refusal for most federal contracts.

"When we initially spoke with government back [in February], we were told, well, you're not going to get the right of first refusal, but we still want to support your organization," said Geoff Hamilton, president and CEO of Commissionaires Great Lakes.
The CRA contract was an outlier in that it was always a competitive bid, but the Commissionaires held the contract until the recent tender.
Aerial view of the Connaught Building, the Canada Revenue Agency's headquarters in Ottawa. (Félix Desroches/Radio-Canada)
Hamilton said the difference in bid was $80,000, representing less than one per cent of the contract's value.
"It is just sort of public sector procurement on autopilot," said Hamilton.
Opposition blasts government over decision
Conservative veterans affairs critic Michael Barrett raised the issue in question period on Tuesday.
"We can all agree that employing Canadian veterans and hiring Canadian companies is important. The question to the Liberals is why didn't they do that in this case?"
Wayne Long, secretary of state for the CRA, both defended the process and argued that cabinet wasn't involved in the decision to go with the private company.
"The process resulted in the selection of a qualified Canadian supplier," Long said in response to Barrett.
"The member knows politicians are never involved in the independent decisions by the CRA."
NDP MP Gord Johns also blasted the decision to award the contract to a private company rather than the Commissionaires.

"Canadians want to know, how does awarding this contract to a foreign owned corporation with those ties [to ICE] instead of a Canadian owned institution supporting veterans square with the Liberals' Canadian promises," Johns said in the House during a debate on military procurement.

In a statement, Allied Universal said it is a registered Canadian company with 10,100 employees and 19 offices across Canada. It said the company's relationship with the U.S. government has existed for several administrations and spans federal agencies.

A spokesperson for Long added in a statement that the CRA's evaluation criteria consider more than overall cost, and can include, among other things, past performance on similar contracts, business continuity planning and ability to recruit and deploy personnel.
The statement said the decisions are made independently, without political interference.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Kate McKenna is a senior reporter with CBC’s parliamentary bureau in Ottawa, where she covers federal politics. She previously worked for CBC’s The Fifth Estate and in the Halifax, Montreal and Charlottetown newsrooms. Her investigative and breaking news coverage has won five RTDNA awards. She is the author of No Choice: The 30-Year Fight for Abortion on Prince Edward Island.

articles.title: Lacson: SC ruling on past budgets timely as Senate reviews 2027 spending plan
articles.summary: Senator Panfilo “Ping” Lacson on Wednesday said the Supreme Court"s ruling declaring provisions of the 2024 and 2025 national budgets unconstitutional came at an opportune time as the Senate…

blocks.text: Published October 21, 2026 4:12am

Senator Panfilo “Ping” Lacson on Wednesday said the Supreme Court’s ruling declaring provisions of the 2024 and 2025 national budgets unconstitutional came at an opportune time as the Senate scrutinizes the House version of the proposed 2027 national budget.
Lacson said the decision underscored the constitutional limits on Congress’ power to increase appropriations recommended by the executive branch in the National Expenditure Program (NEP).

“One good thing about the Supreme Court ruling is its timing. It couldn’t have come at a better time when the House version of the 2027 General Appropriations Bill is undergoing scrutiny by the Senate,” Lacson said in a statement.
He clarified that he was not a senator when Congress passed the 2024 and 2025 General Appropriations Acts.

Lacson earlier warned that the Senate’s review of the proposed 2027 budget could lead to the restoration of “hundreds of billions” of pesos in cuts and realignments made by the House of Representatives, including changes to funding for foreign-assisted projects and additional allocations for flood control.

He also said the Supreme Court ruling placed the 2024 and 2025 budgets among the worst in the country’s history, comparing them with the 2013 national budget provisions involving the Disbursement Acceleration Program (DAP), which the high court also declared unconstitutional.
The Supreme Court, in a 121-page decision, struck down certain provisions of the 2024 and 2025 national budgets, as well as key unprogrammed appropriations in the 2026 budget.

The court ruled that Congress committed grave abuse of discretion when it increased the executive branch’s proposed unprogrammed appropriations from P281.9 billion under the NEP to P731.4 billion in the enacted 2024 budget.

It said Congress is constitutionally prohibited from increasing the president’s total recommended appropriations under the Budget of Expenditures and Sources of Financing, which covers both programmed and unprogrammed appropriations.
Lacson said unspent funds covered by the decision might no longer be disbursed, while expenditures already made might not automatically be invalidated.
“As far as I know, the possible consequences are — those that remain unspent may not be disbursed anymore; those already spent may not be invalidated,” he said.
Salceda

Former Albay lawmaker Joey Salceda welcomed the ruling on the Unprogrammed Appropriations, "particularly its recognition that unprogrammed appropriations are not inherently unconstitutional, but are a legitimate instrument of fiscal management subject to constitutional limits and safeguards."
"The ruling offers an opportunity to move beyond recurring disputes over the national budget and establish a more coherent, transparent, and constitutionally sound budget system," he said.

"The President, who decisively exposed the most glaring abuses of the system, is now in a position to lead that reform, working with Congress to ensure that the flexibility government needs is matched by the accountability the Constitution demands," he added. —LDF, GMA News

articles.title: Zelensky says US intelligence sharing 'works now' after talks with Trump envoy in Oslo
articles.summary: Ukraine had accused the US of withholding key intelligence - a claim rejected as "scandalous" by Washington.

blocks.text: Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky has said US intelligence sharing on deadly Russian missile attacks "works now" after talks with President Donald Trump's special envoy Steve Witkoff.
The meeting in Oslo came after accusations by Kyiv that Washington was withholding key intelligence - a claim rejected as "scandalous" by US Secretary of State Marco Rubio.
Finnish President Alexander Stubb, who also took part in the talks, said "genuine progress" was made on proposals to achieve peace but gave no details and warned that patience would be needed.
Zelensky and his European allies said it was now up to Russia to respond to the proposals agreed in Oslo when Witkoff arrives in St Petersburg on Wednesday.
Witkoff was not present at the joint press conference after Tuesday's talks in the Norwegian capital. Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner, another key envoy, took part in the meeting via video link.

Russian President Vladimir Putin is yet to publicly comment on the latest developments, but Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov earlier said the Kremlin would listen to what Wiktoff would offer, while ruling out "any political concessions".

Relations between Ukraine and the US have soured in recent weeks to the extent that Trump has said it is time for Ukraine to get a new president, and most recently "for somebody else to negotiate on behalf of Ukraine".

Speaking after Zelensky's news conference in Oslo, Trump again told reporters at the White House he wanted Kyiv to "make a deal". He said Russia would like to "get it done" and it was "time for Ukraine to end this war".
Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, and Moscow currently controls about 20% of Ukrainian territory.

Russian drone attacks continued on Tuesday. Ukrainian officials said at least 10 people were killed - four in Kyiv and the capital region, another four in the eastern Donetsk region, and two in the central city of Dnipro.
Addressing the issue of US intelligence sharing after Tuesday's talks, Zelensky said he was "thankful that intelligence works now".

"Speaking about early warning, which is very important for our people, our children, adults, civilians because we can hear when ballistic[s] is coming - so we are thankful to American side, now it works, it's great," the Ukrainian president said.

He said he also hoped for a good result on SpaceX's Starlink satellite access as well, after Ukraine's military had reported in recent days speed restrictions on the US platform used by Kyiv to carry out drone strikes against Russia.
And Zelensky also restated that Ukraine was "ready for negotiations" to end the war.
"Of course, we are not losing this war, but we are losing people because Russia attacks," he said.
The Ukrainian leader added that "strong" security guarantees for Ukraine were also discussed in Oslo, as well as energy ceasefire proposals.
Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre, who also took part in the talks, stressed that Europe "needs to be at the table" during any discussions about how to end the Russia-Ukraine war.
Zelensky took Ukraine's intelligence chief Rustem Umerov and influential lawmaker Davyd Arakhamia with him to Oslo. Both had earlier this month held talks in Miami with Witkoff and Kushner.

Those talks were reportedly ended abruptly when the Ukrainian delegation learned that Trump had announced that Moscow would immediately supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel to the US and other markets, bringing to an end American sanctions on Russian diesel exports.
Zelensky had reacted by calling it "a happy birthday present" for Russian President Vladimir Putin.
Ahead of next month's US midterm elections, Trump has blamed Ukraine's attacks on Russian oil refineries for fuel prices which have been rising since the start of the US-led war on Iran.
Before the Oslo talks, Zelensky said he had had a "constructive discussion" with Rubio about the need for US early warnings, missile interceptors and Starlink.
Last week, a bipartisan group of US senators called for an urgent investigation into speed restrictions to the Starlink network in Ukraine.

Unconfirmed reports earlier on Tuesday said the transfer of more US-made Patriot interceptor missiles - the only effective weapon in shooting down Russian ballistic missiles - had not yet been approved.

Rubio, who is currently on a visit to India, admitted to reporters that it may be true that Patriot interceptors had not yet arrived in Ukraine - but he stressed that nothing had been denied to Kyiv intentionally.
European leaders have expressed concern about recent statements from the US towards Russia.

On Monday, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz spoke of "mixed pictures and messages" on the war, adding that he was trying to convince the American government "in total that this is something we have to resolve jointly".

"It's really a big effort for our budgets, it's really a big thing for the European Union, but we are doing that and we are trying to keep on doing that until this terrible war ends," the German leader told Bloomberg TV.

Asked during an interview on Monday whether or not he saw Ukraine as a US ally, US Vice-President JD Vance said Kyiv was "certainly a partner in some ways, but we have some divergent interests from time to time, like for example... I think they should stop bombing Russian energy".

"We don't have a formal alliance as far as I know with Ukraine. They're not in Nato, I don't think they should be in Nato... we're gonna work together on some things, but also we're going to be opposite on some things too," he said.

articles.title: Trump and Zelensky appear at loggerheads despite Oslo optimism
articles.summary: The Ukrainian leader's hug with Steve Witkoff in the Norwegian capital is unlikely to dispel misgivings about US policy towards his country, writes Paul Adams.

blocks.text: Image source, EPA
Witkoff and Zelensky met in the Norwegian capital
ByPaul Adams
Diplomatic correspondent

The hug that Trump envoy Steve Witkoff offered Volodymyr Zelensky ahead of this afternoon's talks in Oslo is unlikely to have dispelled the Ukrainian leader's misgivings about the current direction of US policy towards his war-ravaged country.
Zelensky posted a video of the moment on social media, with the message "Ukraine is working for peace. I thank our partners for their support!"
But given everything that's happened this month, does the Ukrainian leader still regard Donald Trump as a partner?
The two men have never been close – that much is obvious – but have they now fallen out once and for all?
Both in rhetoric and actions, the past ten days have seen evidence of a rupture as deep as any in their fractious relationship.
Just listen to the way they talk about each other.
"Zelensky's not a good guy for us to deal with," Trump told Newsmax last week.
The verbal assault has continued this week.

"Zelensky doesn't know what he's talking about," Trump told a reporter on Monday when asked what he thought of the Ukrainian leader's suggestion that striking a diesel deal with Russia put the US on the wrong side of history.
Such personal attacks are typical of Trump's sledgehammer approach to diplomacy. It's hard to know when to take them seriously.

In June, he lashed out at Israel's prime minister, saying Benjamin Netanyahu "has no f**king judgement". Four months later, he endorsed Netanyahu enthusiastically, calling him a "great warrior prime minister".
"Trump can always do another U-turn," says Ian Bond of the Centre for European Reform. "But this does look bad."
Watch: Zelensky says US military intelligence sharing "works now"
For his part Zelensky has generally been circumspect in how he describes his unreliable but vital American counterpart.

But this month his frustration has been clear. Addressing a US congressional delegation, he spoke of "decisions on the American side that are hard to explain between friends" and voiced the fear that "some political decision has been made to slow down support for us."
Answering Trump's charge that he represented the principal obstacle to a negotiated settlement, Zelensky sounded more exasperated than ever.
"We have welcomed literally EVERY attempt by our partners to end this war with dignity," he wrote on Telegram on Monday.
But rhetoric aside, how bad is the relationship?
In some ways, we've been here before.

After their notorious televised bust up in the Oval Office in February 2025, at which Trump accused Zelensky of "gambling with World War III", the US suspended military assistance and restricted intelligence sharing.

The crisis only lasted a week. And when the Trump administration decided, later that year, that it no longer wanted to finance direct military assistance to Ukraine, a mechanism was put in place for European countries to pay for American equipment instead.
One exception, in the wake of this year's US war with Iran, has been badly needed US-made Patriot air defence missiles.
Amid a global shortage, the supply to Ukraine has slowed to a trickle, making it harder than ever for Kyiv to shoot down Russian ballistic missiles.

The Washington Post, quoting an unnamed Ukrainian official, said "only a couple" of Patriot interceptors remained in Ukraine's stockpile, and that the Trump administration had slowed down the process by which US allies seek approval to transfer their stocks.
Similar concerns have been voiced in the past, but the latest reports – not confirmed by US officials – come against an increasingly difficult backdrop for Kyiv.

Earlier this month, as Ukrainian negotiators arrived in Miami for talks with Trump's all-purpose envoys Witkoff and Jared Kushner, they were blindsided by the news that the president had just struck a deal with Vladimir Putin to open US markets to Russian diesel.

Experts questioned whether it would do much to drive down US petrol prices, ahead of congressional mid-term elections (the apparent motive), but as a signal of US displeasure over Ukraine's campaign of long-range strikes on Russian oil refineries and Washington's willingness to do deals with the Kremlin, it represented a stinging rebuke to Kyiv.
Watch: 'Time for Ukraine to get a new president', says Trump
Last Friday, Trump went further, waiving wide-ranging sanctions on Russia just two days before they were due to take effect.

Trump said the sanctions contained in the Graham Act (named after the former South Carolina senator Lindsey Graham, a vocal supporter of Ukraine who died in July) would hinder his efforts to broker peace. But for Kyiv and its supporters this was another alarming sign that the White House was siding with the Kremlin.
"What the Trump administration is doing is providing carrots to the Russians and sticks applied to the Ukrainians," former US ambassador to Kyiv William Taylor told the BBC.
"It's inexplicable and saddening."
Kiriil Dmitriev, a senior Putin envoy, called it "an important and truly historic moment".
For Moscow, this felt like a welcome return to the "spirit of Alaska", a phrase much touted by Russian officials in the wake of the Trump-Putin summit in Anchorage in August 2025.

Adding to the impression that Trump is turning his back on Ukraine is the allegation – again not confirmed by Washington – that the US has restricted the flow of intelligence and interfered with Ukraine's access to Elon Musk's Starlink satellite internet service.
Amid an escalation in Russia's drone and missile war on Ukraine's cities, Kyiv says advance warning provided by US satellite intelligence has been lacking.
"We didn't receive it during ballistic attacks for three days," Zelensky told NBC News.
On 12 October five Russian S-400 missiles hit Kyiv, reportedly before air raid sirens or mobile alerts had sounded.
The US Secretary of State, Marco Rubio, denied there had been any pause in intelligence sharing, blaming a "software problem" for the temporary lack of early warnings.
Similar uncertainty surrounds Ukraine's access to Starlink.

A week ago, Ukrainian officials reported that the system was being throttled, with terminals unable to maintain connections at high speeds, making it harder for Ukraine's military to intercept fast moving Russian drones.
Since the summer, Ukraine has struggled to cope with a wave of attacks by advanced, jet-powered drones.
It's not clear where any order to limit Ukraine's use of Starlink – or its military grade equivalent Starshield – originated. Reuters reported that it came from the White House.
Rubio said "no-one at the White House ordered anyone to slow down internet."
But the fact that such suspicions surface so frequently points to the lack of trust that continues to infect US-Ukrainian relations.
Much of this has its roots in Donald Trump's seemingly long-standing mistrust of Ukraine as a whole - and Zelensky in particular.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Russian strikes on Ukraine have continued unabated

blocks.text: Russian strikes on Ukraine have continued unabated

A decade ago, Trump became convinced that Ukraine had tried to prevent him from becoming US president. Among a number of unfounded allegations was the suggestion that the US Democratic National Committee had a server hidden somewhere in Ukraine.
When Zelensky became president, three years later, he resisted Trump's demands that he investigate charges of election interference.
During a notorious July 2019 telephone conversation, Trump also asked Zelensky to investigate Joe Biden, the man who went on to defeat him in the 2020 presidential election. Again, Zelensky refused.
At the time, the White House was withholding $391m (£290m) in military assistance to Ukraine, a juxtaposition that ultimately led to Trump's first impeachment.

Whether Trump's resentment over these historic slights continues to inform his current policy towards Ukraine is an open question, but it's clear that the roller coaster of US-Ukraine relations has taken another stomach-churning dip.
Following the talks in Oslo, Witkoff is taking a set of updated proposals to St Petersburg. All eyes will now be on Putin.
Jonas Gahr Støre, the Norwegian leader, said the talks in Oslo had helped "to straighten out a few things."
"There's nothing to gain from… digging into what was said yesterday or a week ago," he said diplomatically.

Zelensky said the day had begun with a productive conversation with the US Secretary of State and indicated that the issue of early warning had already been fixed. He also sounded optimistic about Patriot missiles and Starlink.
"I think we will have good results too," he said.
Yet despite the optimistic tone, it's hard to get around the fact that Volodymyr Zelensky and Donald Trump appear, once again, to be at loggerheads.

articles.title: Lawsuit challenging Trump's tariffs against Canada filed in U.S. Court of International Trade
articles.summary: A lawsuit challenging U.S. President Donald Trump's tariffs targeting Canada has been filed in the United States Court of International Trade.

image.caption: A lawsuit challenging U.S. President Donald Trump's tariffs on Canada was filed in the U.S. Court of International Trade Tuesday. (Mark Schiefelbein/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: World
A lawsuit challenging U.S. President Donald Trump's tariffs targeting Canada has been filed in the United States Court of International Trade.
Case was filed by the Liberty Justice Center on behalf of a U.S. business
· The Canadian Press
· Posted: Oct 20, 2026 3:59 PM EDT | Last Updated: 16 minutes ago

The lawsuit, filed Tuesday by the non-profit Liberty Justice Center on behalf of U.S. food importer Gellert Global Group, argues Trump's use of a Depression-era trade statute exceeds his power as president.

"Using the Section 338, which is, in my opinion, a dormant statute from 1930 that has never been used before, just said to us that this is wrong and we should do something about it," Liberty Justice Center CEO Sara Albrecht said in an interview from Chicago with CBC's Katie Simpson.
Trump used Section 338 to slap an array of Canadian goods with a 50 per cent levy after trade talks broke down in August.
The same statute was used the following month to ban the import of other Canadian goods, including motorcycles and some alcohol and dairy products.
Lawsuit argues Canadian policies don't justify tariffs

The White House has said Section 338 empowers the president to impose tariffs when a country puts U.S. exporters at a disadvantage relative to exporters in other countries — even though the law has never been used for that purpose.
U.S. officials have said the latest duties are a response to provincial bans on U.S. liquor, Canada's supply managed dairy system and quotas on certain U.S. vehicles.
Tuesday's lawsuit said the Canadian policies don't justify the sweeping tariffs imposed by the Trump administration.

items: Trump says 'very bad' Canada is being 'taught a little lesson' as trade action escalates
Fact-checking the White House statement of facts about Canada

blocks.text: It notes two of the measures — auto quotas and liquor bans — were actually a response to Trump's own tariff measures.

The lawsuit also said Canada's dairy supply management involves policies agreed to under the Canada-U.S.-Mexico Agreement on trade, known as CUSMA, which was negotiated during the first Trump administration.

"This has real world consequences on not just the importers but the consumers in both countries," Albrecht said. "And I think it has even broader implications given the nature of the two countries and our historical relationship to each other."
She said she accepts that tariffs are one of Trump's signature policies, but says the way they are being implemented in this case is wrong.
"He has always been in love with tariffs, in my opinion, primarily because it's revenue … I can respect that," Albrecht said. "But in this case, it's wrong and it's violating our Constitution."
Feds have hired 'best lawyers' to advise on Stelco next steps, says Joly

A Trump administration official, commenting on background, said the president's actions will be vigorously defended in court. The official said Tuesday's lawsuit won't deter the president's commitment to levelling the playing field for American workers, farmers and firms.
Concerns beyond Canada
But in the meantime, the Trump administration's actions are leading to consequences for American businesses.

Thomas Gellert, co-chief executive officer of Gellert Global Group, said the company has "spent generations building trusted relationships with suppliers, customers and partners across the food industry."
"These tariffs disrupt those relationships overnight and create costs and uncertainty that ripple through the entire supply chain," Gellert said in the news release.

The company is being hit by the trade war on all sides, it goes on to say. It pays a 50 per cent tariff on imports of Canadian cheese but is also slammed by Ottawa's retaliatory tariffs on the American-made cheeses that its Canadian division sells in Canada.

The company cites the experience of one of its Canadian cheese suppliers to show how the integrated North American market is being disrupted by the tariff dispute. It gets milk from dairy farmers in Upstate New York, which is processed into brie in Canada, which is then sent back to the United States.
"The tariffs hit American farmers and businesses on both sides of that transaction," the news release said.

The case raises concerns beyond Canada, the news release said. If the duties remain unchecked, any president could use Section 338 to impose tariffs and trade restrictions without meaningful congressional control.
The lawsuit asks the court to declare the tariffs unlawful and order a refund.

The Liberty Justice Center was previously involved in the legal challenge against Trump's use of the International Economic Emergency Powers Act of 1977 for the so-called "Liberation Day" and fentanyl-related tariffs on Canada, Mexico and China.
In February, America's top court concluded it was not legal for Trump to use the statute, known as IEEPA, because the U.S. Constitution very clearly gives Congress power over taxes and tariffs.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Kelly Geraldine Malone is a reporter for The Canadian Press.
With files from CBC's Katie Simpson

articles.title: Zelenskyy visits Norway amid Trump White House tensions
articles.summary: Ukrainian President Zelenskyy met with Norwegian and Finnish leaders in Oslo and held talks with Trump envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner. Trump is pressuring Zelenskyy to "make a deal" with…

image.caption: Zelenskyy hugged US envoy Steve Witkoff at the meeting with Finnish and Norwegian leaders looking on Image: Heiko Junge/NTB/AFP

blocks.text: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy visited Norway on Tuesday as Ukraine faces renewed tension in its relationship with US President Donald Trump and his administration.
Finland's Stubb: 'Today was a good day for peace'

During the visit, Zelenskyy met with Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store in Oslo, along with Trump envoy Steve Witkoff. The US president's son-in-law, Jared Kushner, joined the meeting remotely.
Store described the meeting involving the European and the US sides as "good and constructive" at a press conference.
"US and European teams have done substantive work on key issues together with Ukraine," Store said.
Stubb said, "Today was a good day for peace." The Finnish president said Witkoff intends to fly to St. Petersburg on Wednesday to meet with Russian leaders and discuss ideas from the Oslo meeting.

blocks.caption: Trump envoy Steve Witkoff was not present at the press conference after the meeting Image: Jonathan Nackstrand/AFP

blocks.text: The Oslo meeting comes as Zelenskyy has accused the US of withholding intelligence from Ukraine in advance of Russian strikes and delaying the delivery of interceptor missiles.
Zelenskyy: Early intel warnings from partners on Russian strikes resume
Zelenskyy said he held a phone call with US Secretary of State Marco Rubio earlier in the day and said Ukraine is now receiving early warnings from its partners ahead of Russian strikes.

"We are thankful that intelligence works now, and I'm speaking about early warning, which is very important for our people, for children, adults, civilians, because we can hear when ballistic is coming," Zelenskyy said of the Russian-launched missiles while standing next to Finnish and Norwegian leaders.
There are also media reports that Trump, Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping could hold a meeting to possibly discuss Ukraine and other issues.

"I don't know what the trilateral meeting will be about between America and China, and Russia, it's up to them," Zelenskyy said, but added that if Ukraine is discussed, it would be acceptable only if Ukrainians are at the negotiating table.
Trump ramps up attacks on Zelenskyy as US midterms loom

Earlier this month, Zelenskyy criticized a deal struck between the Trump administration and Russia to buy Russian diesel fuel. Oil and gas export revenues are vital for the Russian economy and war efforts in Ukraine.
How Trump is helping Putin

Trump has criticized Zelenskyy and blamed Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries for high diesel prices. Prices have increased dramatically since Iran closed the Strait of Hormuz in response to US attacks.

Zelenskyy on Tuesday said he is supportive of Trump's suggestion to stop attacks on energy sites, with Russia also doing the same in regard to Ukraine as part of an "energy ceasefire." However, Zelenskyy said Russia is unwilling to stop its attacks on Ukraine.
At a recent European Union summit in Brussels, Zelenskyy smiled at the suggestion that he is being made a scapegoat by Trump.

The US president is looking for someone else to blame for high domestic energy costs ahead of midterm congressional elections onb November 3. If the opposition Democrats take back control of the US House and Senate, it could constrain Trump's powers in his last two years in office.
In comments to reporters at the White House on Tuesday, Trump said he wants Zelenskyy to "make a deal" with Russia and suggested Moscow has the upper hand.

Ukraine has been fighting off a full-scale Russian invasion since February 2022. In the past, Trump has blamed Zelenskyy for the war and on Tuesday again said it was up to Kyiv to end the Russian invasion.
“We want Zelenskyy to make a deal,” Trump told reporters in the Oval Office. “We’ve given a lot to Ukraine. We’ve gotten absolutely nothing back except grief, death, tremendous monetary loss.”
Trump said he also spoke with Putin about Stephen Hubbard, a retired US teacher detained in Russia accused of acting as a mercenary for Ukrainian forces.
"I've been talking to President Putin about Mr. Hubbard. I've been talking to him at length. I've asked him to release him. Let's see what happens," Trump said.
