articles.title: EXPLAINER: Which jobs are most vulnerable to AI replacement?
articles.summary: Among the industries that will be most impacted by AI are business process outsourcing and information technology, which are among the major employers in the Philippines.

blocks.text: While the rise of artificial intelligence (AI) has presented new opportunities, its developments have raised concerns about its impact on human labor.

In a report from GMA News Feed, voice-over artist Inka Magnaye's post about how her mother lost an acting job to AI went viral. Magnaye said that while AI is an instrument, it should not be used to replace human talent.
Workers across different industries have echoed this sentiment. But which jobs are in danger of being affected by AI?
According to the Tokyo-based think tank Asian Development Bank Institute (ADBI), 76% of work in the Philippines will be highly vulnerable to automation by the year 2030—the highest in Southeast Asia.
Among the industries that will be most impacted are business process outsourcing and information technology, which are among the major employers in the Philippines.

The Information Technology and Business Process Association of the Philippines (IBPAP) said that the industry is also expecting lower revenue. In its six-year roadmap in 2022, the industry was targeted to generate $59 billion in revenues. However, as of July 2026, this has been lowered to $43 billion to $50 billion.

The IBPAP was also expecting 2.5 million workers to be employed in the industry by 2028. But a review of the roadmap led to the projection being lowered to 1.85 million to 2.14 million. These workers, however, have switched to different employment.

"It has affected some jobs, but based on all the members we’ve talked to, the entry-level jobs that some of the AI trials have affected, those employees have been able to be redeployed,” IBPAP president Jack Madrid said.

The International Labour Organization (ILO) said that around 12.7 million workers in the Philippines have been exposed to generative AI—a type of AI that could make its own text, image, audio, video and computer code.
This does not mean that AI will replace workers immediately; tasks will just become automated.
However, 3.6% of jobs with the highest use of generative AI have a higher chance of job displacement.

According to the International Confederation of Societies of Authors and Composers, the revenue of the music industry could be reduced by 24%, with audiovisual creators also seeing a reduction of 21% in revenue.
AI ethicist Carl Joe Javier said that this could have a greater effect on Filipino creatives.

“If we have arts, which historically have been undervalued, and then you have tech movements, which also push to undervalue art, because they're like, “I don't need artists anymore because this thing can generate images for me.” Because the tech people, they actually don't really care about art. That's not their concern. They don't care about cultural preservation,” Javier said.

Javier said that a number of companies use AI to cut costs. However, is saving money worth risking the quality of the output that a human can do? Would it be possible to put together what a human and AI could do to improve the output?

“When everyone had a computer, look at the productivity, the productivity gains. When you go to the office, and everyone has a computer. Because in the old days, not everyone was assigned a computer. Now that we all have smartphones, we are more productive than we ever were. But none of those devices involved the removal of people,” he said.

Many experts still believe that AI could not replace humans in the workplace. The Harvard Business School said that AI does not have emotional intelligence to solve interpersonal conflict or understand human behavior.
Only humans could make a human connection. AI could still help lighten the load, however.
The ILO had suggested targeting regional and sectoral policies to make sure that people could benefit from generative AI. Workers should be prepared for the changes that this technology could bring.
Workers vulnerable to AI replacement should also be protected.

“I do think that everyone should be pressuring their legislators to pass legislation and regulation. And hindi lang parang may budget for upskilling…All these technologies continue to change the world; how are we going to imagine and situate ourselves within this world? And how are we going to imagine our workforce and our economy within that context? So, kailangan, sana, we have people who are pushing in that direction,” Javier said. —Jean Mangaluz/LDF, GMA News

articles.title: Lebanon faces uncertainty as UNIFIL mandate nears end
articles.summary: As UN peacekeeping forces prepare to withdraw from Lebanon, Israel remains present and Hezbollah is still armed. A new EU support mission aims to strengthen Lebanon's army, but will not replace UN…

image.caption: Thousands of troops are due to leave Lebanon as the UNIFIL mandate ends on December 31, 2026, prompting fears of a security vacuum Image: Mahmoud Zayyat/AFP

blocks.text: As the mandate of the United Nations Interim Force in Lebanon, or UNIFIL, nears its end, uncertainty over the future of southern Lebanon is growing. Lebanese Prime Minister Nawaf Salam has warned of the need to "avert the vacuum that UNIFIL's withdrawal could create, were it to take place without agreement on a new international force to replace it."

The Lebanese government has also been pushing for a last-minute extension of UNIFIL's mandate, but so far without success. It is most likely that the 7,565 peacekeepers from 46 countries will begin withdrawing from the UN-patrolled so-called Blue Line zone on December 31, 2026.

The Blue Line, which stretches for 120 kilometers (75 miles), is a UN-identified line of withdrawal between Israel and Lebanon, not an internationally agreed border. It was established in 2000. However, as early as in 1978, multinational UNIFIL troops were deployed to this region to monitor the area after Israel invaded Lebanon in response to attacks by Palestinian armed groups.

After the 2006 Israel-Hezbollah war, the mandate was expanded to support the Lebanese army in implementing UN Security Council Resolution 1701. The resolution calls for an area between the Blue Line and the Litani River to be free of armed personnel, assets and weapons other than those belonging to the Lebanese government and UNIFIL. It also calls for the withdrawal of Israeli forces from southern Lebanon.

However, following cross-border attacks by Hezbollah in October 2023 and the ensuing war in 2024, Israel has been occupying large swaths of Lebanese territory in a self-declared security zone called the Yellow Line, which is located north of the Blue Line.

Of the more than 1.2 million people displaced in Lebanon during the renewed conflict in 2026, around 329,000 remained internally displaced as of September 29, according to the International Organization for Migration. Israel has also caused extensive destruction to homes and key infrastructure in southern Lebanon, saying it needs to protect its citizens in northern Israel from attacks launched from the area.

Hezbollah — which is designated as a terrorist organization by several countries, including the United States and Germany, while the European Union designates its armed wing as a terrorist organization — continues to reject disarmament, citing the need to defend itself for as long as Israeli forces remain in Lebanon.
Hezbollah is also closely linked to Iran, and in case of renewed conflict between Iran and Israel, it's likely that Hezbollah would open a second front in Israel's north in support of Iran.

blocks.caption: Around 1.2 million people were displaced in Lebanon this year. However, the majority have since returned to their homes in the southImage: Mohammed Zaatari/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: "The situation in southern Lebanon remains tense," Kandice Ardiel, UNIFIL's spokesperson, told DW. "We are seeing continued Israeli military operations, including overflights of Lebanese airspace by jets, helicopters and drones, airstrikes, artillery strikes and mortar fire."

"Until our mandate ends on December 31, we continue to monitor and report what is happening, and we are liaising between the parties on a daily basis to ensure safe movements of civilians, humanitarian aid, and peacekeeping patrols," she said, adding that the drawdown and withdrawal would then take place in stages.

The end of the mandate also means the end of the mission for thousands of UNIFIL troops in southern Lebanon. "People have built careers, friendships, skills and a sense of purpose together," Ardiel said. "Endings are never easy, especially when there is a sense that the work we do is still needed."
Beirut's lack of authority, money compounds disarmament dilemma
The upcoming withdrawal of UNIFIL also highlights two major dilemmas for Lebanon's government.

"Beirut is concerned that violations of any agreements, whether on the Israeli or the Hezbollah side, can't be tracked in the absence of an international military force," Paul Shaya, a Washington-based Middle East researcher and adjunct professor at George Washington University, told DW.

Furthermore, after years of political deadlock, the COVID-19 pandemic, soaring inflation and economic crises, the Beirut port blast in 2020 and the destruction caused by the 2024 war between Israel and Hezbollah, Lebanon's economic lifeline depends on international funding. However, a large share of the much-needed investment from the United States and Gulf states is tied to Hezbollah's disarmament.
"Ultimately, it is going to be dependent on President Joseph Aoun and Prime Minister Nawaf Salam to secure sufficient funding and resources to support the Lebanese military," said Shaya.
Can Lebanon's peace experiment work?

Until that happens, Aoun and Salam have very limited options for disarming Hezbollah, said David Wood, Lebanon researcher at the International Crisis Group. "They have opened direct talks with Israel to bring about an end to the disastrous conflict, but that process includes neither Hezbollah nor its backer Iran — both of which oppose the group's disarmament," he said.

In Wood's view, Beirut has few bargaining chips in negotiations with Israel because it has been unable to secure Hezbollah's compliance. He is also worried that Lebanon's leaders have little leverage to force Hezbollah to surrender its weapons, as this could trigger a deadly domestic conflict in the country. In the past, Hezbollah has openly warned that trying to seize its weapons by force would lead to war.

Despite Israel's destruction of many Hezbollah tunnels and weapons-storage facilities in Hezbollah-dominated areas in southern Lebanon and parts of Beirut, the limitation or disruption of supply routes due to the wider Iran war, as well as the fall of their ally, Syrian President Bashar Assad, observers say Hezbollah remains better equipped than the Lebanese armed forces.
Could the new EU mission replace UNIFIL in Lebanon?
On October 12, European Union foreign ministers agreed to establish a European Union Support Mission in Lebanon, or EUSM Lebanon, with an initial three-year mandate.
"It has a civilian and military pillar," EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said, adding that "this is highly welcomed by the local authorities."

blocks.caption: The Iran-backed Hezbollah group maintains a political arm as well as a military arm in LebanonImage: Hussein Malla/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: According to the European Council, the mission is to contribute to peace and security in Lebanon by strengthening the capabilities of the Lebanese armed forces and internal security forces, including in border security in accordance with the UN Security Council Resolution 1701.
However, the mission is not intended to replace UNIFIL. Rather than deploying peacekeepers to patrol southern Lebanon, it is set to initially operate north of the Litani River.

Several existing UNIFIL contributors, including Italy, France, Spain, Ireland, Germany, Austria, Finland and Poland, already expressed interest in contributing personnel and resources to the new EUSM Lebanon mission.

For the government in Beirut, this is a positive signal, noted Shaya. He added that Lebanese society also strongly supports the Lebanese military, "which many see as the only institution in the country that can uphold Lebanon's sovereignty and represent the entire country."

articles.title: Sudan drone strike kills around 150 in Abyei market
articles.summary: A drone strike hit a market in the Abyei border region disputed by Sudan and South Sudan and killed dozens. The drone caused a large fire when it hit a fuel depot. South Sudanese officials blamed…

image.caption: Medical workers, including from Medecins Sans Frontieres, worked to treat the wounded at the nearby Ameth Bek hospitalImage: Medecins Sans Frontieres/REUTERS

blocks.text: A drone strike in a busy market in the disputed region of Abyei has killed more than 150 people, according to local officials.

South Sudanese officials blamed Sudan's military for the attack, without providing evidence, amid the long-running civil war between the Sudanese Armed Forces and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) militia, which is reportedly active in the Abyei area.

The special UN mission in Abyei warned in May that the RSF's presence in the resource-rich region had put residents in additional danger, and risked intensifying the older territorial dispute between Sudan and the world's newest sovereign state, South Sudan.

blocks.caption: Satellite images gave a sense of the scale of the damage after the large fire triggered by the drone strikesImage: Planet Labs PBC/REUTERS

blocks.text: What do we know about the drone strike?
According to local authorities, the attack hit the busy Amiet Market at around midday on Monday.

Yohana Akol Ngor, the caretaker information minister in Abyei, told Reuters news agency on Tuesday that the death toll had more than doubled, reaching at least 153 compared to a stated figure of 73 the previous day.
He said that Sudan's military was responsible for the attack but did not provide evidence. Akol Ngor said around 8,000 people had been displaced by the bombing.
South Sudan's Foreign Ministry also blamed the Sudanese army and said the drone struck multiple locations around the busy market.
One of these, judging by witness accounts, was a fuel depot — and this led to a large fire that proved difficult to bring under control overnight and was still ablaze on Tuesday.
South Sudan said it had summoned Sudan's ambassador to protest and urged Sudan to "refrain from any actions that endanger civilian lives and property."
Medical charity Medecins Sans Frontieres (MSF), or Doctors Without Borders, said that its staff was treating some 20 wounded people at the nearby Ameth Bek hospital.
"So far we received over 20 patients, including several critical cases. Patients with burns were also admitted," said Dr. Christian Lindauer, MSF's medical activities manager at the hospital.

blocks.caption: Many of the wounded were taken to Ameth Bek hospital for treatmentImage: Medecins Sans Frontieres/REUTERS

blocks.text: What's the backstory of Sudan, South Sudan and Abyei?
The oil-rich Abyei region's status was not resolved by the 2005 peace agreement that broadly ended decades of civil war in Sudan.
It was also not settled in 2011 when South Sudan became an independent country.

A referendum was planned but never materialized, stalling over disputes on who should be allowed to vote. This left Abyei in a state of limbo, jointly administered and with an interim UN security force on site for 15 years.
The region's majority Ngok Dinka population favors joining South Sudan, while Misseriya nomads who use its pastures favor Sudan.
Amiet Market, the site of the attack, is an important trading hub for both communities.
The unstable region has also experienced intercommunal violence in recent years between Ngok Dinka and neighboring Twic Dinka communities and is home to other armed militias.

blocks.caption: Medecins Sans Frontieres said its staff were providing surgical services, wound dressing and other emergency care to more than 20 woundedImage: Medecins Sans Frontieres/REUTERS

blocks.text: How does this fit into Sudan's army's war with the RSF?

The April 2023 outbreak of fighting between the Sudanese Armed Forces and the Rapid Support Forces paramilitary — which has turned into a conflict with fairly entrenched battle lines, putting Sudan into a de facto state of partition — is increasing tension in the already-strained region.
Abyei borders South Kordofan state in Sudan, which has become a major center of fighting in the war.
Sudan's military alleges that the RSF is also operating out of Abyei. The United Nations Interim Security Force for Abyei (UNISFA) issued a similar statement in May.
Officials in Abyei and South Sudan dispute this, however.
Sudan's military and the RSF have both been using drones extensively in the conflict.

"We remain alarmed by the relentless drone attacks across Sudan, as well as the damage they are causing to critical infrastructure — these attacks are taking a devastating toll on communities already struggling with the consequences of more than three years of conflict," UN spokesperson Stephane Dujarric told reporters in New York on Tuesday when asked about the attack.
Sudan's civil war — the limits of humanitarian aid

articles.title: Staying in Canada is a 'huge relief' for Alberta business leaders
articles.summary: With a resounding vote in favour of Alberta staying in Canada, business leaders are breathing easier, saying the result of the provincial referendum will bring more certainty for investors and give a…

image.caption: A supporter writes on a protest sign during a pro-Canada rally in Edmonton, on Sunday. Business leaders on Tuesday cheered the vote for Alberta to remain in Canada. (Timon Johnson/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Business

With a resounding vote in favour of Alberta staying in Canada, business leaders are breathing easier, saying the result of the provincial referendum will bring more certainty for investors and give a boost to the entire country's economy.
'Certainty has been established,' says head of Calgary Chamber of Commerce
"It is a huge relief," said Deborah Yedlin, president and CEO of the Calgary Chamber of Commerce.
"This vote to stay in Canada means that certainty has been established and that we can attract that investment. And that will benefit the economy, not just for Alberta, but for the country."
Albertans voted on 10 questions on Monday, one of which asked whether voters wanted the province to remain in Canada, or if they were in favour of holding a binding referendum on whether to separate.

Ballots are still being counted, but with 1.8 million votes tallied 12 hours after polls closed, the remain side was leading with 75.5 per cent, and CBC News is projecting that Albertans have voted to remain in Canada.

For some, economic challenges within the province were part of the reason for wanting to separate. The crash in oil prices in 2014 hit the major energy-producing province hard, and supporters of separation have said they could reap more benefits from the oil patch if Alberta were on its own and didn't have to make equalization payments to the rest of Canada.
Deborah Yedlin, president and CEO of the Calgary Chamber of Commerce, says the result of the vote is a major relief for business owners and investors in the province and abroad. (Joe Fiorino/CBC)

But many business leaders ahead of the referendum voiced their support for the remain side. The Canadian Chamber of Commerce and Alberta Chamber of Commerce warned in July that a yes vote for a future binding referendum could open "another cycle of uncertainty" for business owners, leading potential investors to stay on the sidelines until the dust had settled on whether the province would leave Canada.

items: Albertans vote to remain in Canada, CBC News projects
Economic frustration helps fuel Alberta separatism — and these 4 charts suggest why

blocks.text: A poll of the Calgary Chamber of Commerce's members found that nearly half of respondents said they were prepared to relocate their businesses outside of the province if Albertans voted to begin the formal process to leave the country. And another 60 per cent in that same poll said that separatism was already taking a negative toll on their business.

With the vote coming at a time of widespread global uncertainty and a worsening trade relationship between the U.S. and Canada, Yedlin said the referendum question only "added to the pile" for business leaders.

At Capital Power, CEO Avik Dey says he wasn't holding off on making any business decisions because of the referendum, but that the separation question did cause some anxiety for investors outside of the province.
"This has absolutely been some level of overhang for us. And I think that overhang dissipates this morning," Dey said.
Alberta is rich. So why are so many people frustrated?
Potential impact of lingering separatist sentiment

Charles St-Arnaud, chief economist with Alberta-based Servus Credit Union, agrees that with the immediate uncertainty lifted, things will get back to "business as usual" for any investors who had been taking a wait-and-see approach ahead of the vote.

But separatists have vowed to keep fighting for an independent Alberta despite the result. And with some 25 per cent still in favour of holding a binding vote on whether to leave the country, St-Arnaud says the referendum may not be the last word on separation, meaning the drag on businesses could persist.

items: 'Never giving up': Alberta separatist leaders say referendum vote won't end their fight

blocks.text: "The problem is … how does it distract the business community and policymakers and the government in terms of thinking about putting the right policies, right decisions in place?" St-Arnaud said.

St-Arnaud, who lived in Montreal during the 1995 Quebec referendum, says questions of independence persisted in that province and weighed on business activity for years following that province's independence vote. He says whether the separatist conversation in Alberta has an impact on investment going forward will depend on whether it remains part of mainstream politics.
'We've started the dialogue,' Alberta separatist campaigner says of referendum

Canadian Chamber of Commerce president and CEO Candace Laing acknowledged the concerns of separatists, which she said need to be addressed in order to build a strong and united Canadian economy going forward.

"Alberta is central to economic security and opportunity in Canada and we must now turn our attention squarely to the needed work to collaboratively build a stronger, resilient, united economy from coast to coast to coast," Laing said.
But with Albertans "clearly" deciding to remain in Canada, by Laing's read of the vote, she was optimistic that the result would be taken as a positive sign by business leaders and investors alike.
"Businesses, workers and communities can feel more confident with this result," Laing said. "Let's move forward, stronger together."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Abby Hughes is a writer with CBC News based in Toronto. Originally from Orillia, Ont., she studied journalism at Toronto Metropolitan University. She covers news from the worlds of business, entertainment, health, science and education, and her favourite stories focus on the real people in those areas — the customers, fans, patients, citizens and students. You can reach her with story ideas at abby.hughes@cbc.ca.
With files from Kyle Bakx, Ina Sidhu and Meegan Read

articles.title: Nato increases Black Sea deployment amid escalating deadly Russian attacks
articles.summary:
Mounting anxiety as Russia’s war on Ukraine reaches Nato’s borders with targeting of vessels transporting agricultural cargo

Nato is deploying additional military assets to the Black Sea…

blocks.text: Nato is deploying additional military assets to the Black Sea amid the recent deadly escalation of Russian attacks on merchant shipping, as five more vessels were attacked on Tuesday.
Russia’s military said it ⁠struck ​three cargo vessels in Ukraine’s ⁠port of Reni and two ⁠other cargo vessels en ​route ‌to ‌Odesa.

Russia’s targeting of vessels taking grain and other agricultural cargoes from Ukraine’s ports – central to the country’s economy – have brought the conflict to Nato’s borders, with a new high-risk designation used by the London shipping insurance market now covering all of the Black Sea save for the territorial waters of Romania, Bulgaria and Turkey.

With a sharply rising death toll among civilian seafarers that has made Black Sea routes the world’s most dangerous, Nato announced the ⁠defensive military alliance would add more surveillance assets in the region.

Nato’s spokesperson, Allison Hart, said: “Today, Nato ‌ambassadors met in ‌the North Atlantic Council to discuss security in the Black Sea. Nato has already ​strengthened our posture along the eastern flank, including with counter-drone ⁠capabilities. Nato will ​be sending ​additional assets ​to the region, ​including ‌support for surveillance, ​reconnaissance, ​and forensics.”

The deployment will include maritime patrol aircraft, radar systems, drones and intelligence personnel. There is mounting anxiety about the increasing overspill from Russia’s war on Ukraine and the potential for further friction with Nato.

Concern has been growing after alleged Russian attacks that have increasingly edged into the territorial waters and exclusive economic zones of Bulgaria and Romania. Romania deployed jets over the weekend to shoot down two suspected Russian drones over its territory.

blocks.caption: A vessel that was hit by a drone in the Black Sea this month. Photograph: Bulgarian Interior Ministry/Reuters

blocks.text: Romania’s defence minister, Radu Miruță, said the drones were probably latest generation Russian drones, flying at speeds similar to fighter jets.

“The ones from last night were flying ​at 450 km/h, which leads us to think they were Russian-made Geran-4 drones with a turboprop ​engine,” Miruță said. “This is the first time we’ve shot down drones like these.”
Romania has recorded 35 unauthorised drone incursions so far this year, compared with nine in 2025. Romanian forces have downed six drones this year, compared with zero last year.

Last week, two chemical tankers were hit by drones near Romania’s Black Sea coast, the latest ​in a series of attacks that have highlighted the risks to commercial shipping on Nato’s eastern flank. Both vessels were anchored near ​the Sulina canal, which links the Danube River to the Black Sea and is an export route for Ukraine.

At least five other cargo ships have been hit near the coasts of Romania and Bulgaria in the ​past two weeks, with 23 sailors reported dead or missing. Most of those incidents ​occurred outside ⁠Nato territorial waters.

blocks.caption: Four rescued sailors arrive in Bulgaria after their vessel sank following an attack in the Black Sea this month.  Photograph: Denislav Stoychev/NurPhoto/Shutterstock

blocks.text: Amid mounting concern, Bulgaria has asked Nato for the deployment of combat aircraft and anti-drone systems to its territory. On 18 October, France sent a maritime reconnaissance aircraft to Romania.

The maritime insurer and risk analyst Ambrey has said there is no end in sight to the threats to Black Sea cargo shipping, including grain and oil, and that insurance prices for passage of the waters have rocketed.

Tomas Alexa, a senior analyst at Ambrey, said last week his company had noted a sharp increase in the tempo of attacks beginning in July. Russian forces are estimated to be responsible for 80% of them.

The recent loss of life, he suggested, had been exacerbated by “double tap” attacks involving aerial and surface drones, the latter often carrying up to half a tonne of explosive payloads. Smaller vessels that primarily use the Danube canal system have sunk rapidly.
“While attacks against merchant vessels in the Black Sea are not new, we are seeing an escalation both in terms of the number of attacks and in the geographical scope,” Alexa said.

articles.title: You Can See Everything launches ambitious Oscars campaign
articles.summary: A24 has launched a head-turning Oscars campaign for the film You Can See Everything, which highlights how unusual the documentary is.

image.caption: Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes appears in a still from the documentary, You Can See Everything. (A24)

blocks.text: Entertainment·New
A24 has launched a head-turning Oscars campaign for the film You Can See Everything, which highlights how unusual the documentary is.
A24 pushes for documentary to be nominated in Best Picture category
There's no question You Can See Everything is generating a lot of buzz. But will it translate into Oscars buzz?
The film distributor, A24, certainly hopes so.
In fact, the company has launched an awards campaign that's turning a lot of industry heads.

Even those who haven't seen the film yet are probably familiar with You Can See Everything's premise: 34 days before she’s sent to prison, Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes invites a skeptical film crew to document her every move.

In 2014, Holmes made multi-millions by claiming she had developed a technology that could cheaply screen for hundreds of diseases using just a few drops of blood from a finger prick. By 2022, Theranos had been dissolved and Holmes was convicted of wire fraud and conspiracy to defraud investors.

The film begins as a documentary-style portrait of an enigmatic felon and becomes something much different. Those who have seen it describe it as some variation of mind-blowing, a fever dream or unlike anything they've seen before.
So it's no surprise You Can See Everything is campaigning to be nominated for Best Documentary — a category Canada has historically done very well in.
What's more surprising is A24 wants the film to be considered for Best Picture.
Nathan Fielder searches for truth in You Can See Everything
In the Academy Awards' 98-year history, no feature documentary has ever been nominated for Best Picture.

And that's not the only big fish You Can See Everything is eyeing. It is putting Lance Oppenheim and Canadian Nathan Fielder forward to be considered in the Best Directory category. Again, something no documentary has ever accomplished.

You Can See Everything has put forward two Canadian names for consideration in the categories of Best Cinematography (David Bolen) and Best Film Editing (Adam Locke-Norton), plus others for Best Original Score, Best Sound and Best Production Design.
Warning: spoilers start here

To those unfamiliar with the film, here's where things start to get a little head-scratchy: A24's awards page suggests the film also deserves nominations for Best Costume Design (another Canadian name, Katina Danabassis, here) as well as Best Makeup and Hairstyling.
Yes. For a documentary.
If you've seen it, you understand why. If you haven't, you'll be even more surprised by this next category.
Variety has reported there is another campaign — one not listed on A24's awards page — for Amanda Seyfried to be nominated as Best Supporting Actress.
Seyfried played the documentary's subject, Elizabeth Holmes, in the 2022 TV miniseries The Dropout. She appears in You Can See Everything as herself, reprising the role of Holmes.
It's all very meta, and might make your shake your head a bit, but Variety has confirmed Seyfried would indeed be eligible for an acting nomination.

items: You Can See Everything sells out theatres, and people can't stop talking about it
Nathan Fielder's You Can See Everything gazes into the abyss of Elizabeth Holmes

blocks.text: Judging by the rave reviews, audiences are loving how You Can See Everything has pushed the boundaries of filmmaking.

We'll see if the Academy of Motion Pictures Arts and Sciences has the same appreciation for the fearless approach to awards season on Jan. 21 of next year. That's when The Oscar nominations are due to be announced.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Helen Surgenor is a producer for CBC News based in Toronto, currently working for the entertainment unit. She spent years waking up before dawn to make the daily news podcast World Report. She has reported in Alberta, Iqaluit and Barbados. You can reach her at helen.surgenor@cbc.ca.

articles.title: COA flags AICs double beneficiaries; DSWD says no funds wasted
articles.summary: The COA flagged what it saw as DSWD double beneficiaries in 2025, but the latter agency maintained that there were no funds wasted and most of the issues had a sound explanation.

blocks.text: Published October 21, 2026 1:28am

The Commission on Audit (COA) flagged what it saw as the Department of Social Welfare and Development’s (DSWD) double beneficiaries in 2025, but the latter agency maintained that there were no funds wasted and most of the issues had a sound explanation.

In a 24 Oras report from Darlene Cay, COA had flagged 5,000 beneficiaries that received double the amount from the Assistance to Individuals in Crisis Situations (AICS) program, with around 400,000 people receiving more than their entitled cash benefits.

According to COA, this resulted in P397.5 million more given out than was meant to be disbursed. There were also 6,000 people who received AICS even if they already got aid from the Ayuda para sa Kapos ang Kita Program (AKAP).
There were also more than 1,000 people who received cash aid multiple times, which led to COA flagging P9 million in suspicious claims.
However, the DSWD said that there were no funds wasted.

“COA never pointed any ghost beneficiaries. COA never pointed any deficiency na ninakaw ng empleyado. Walang ganun. And if they point it out, we will see to it na ma-aksiyunan namin… Wala kami ng notice of suspension. They are cross-checking the validation as well,” Social Welfare Secretary Rex Gatchalian said.

(COA never pointed out any ghost beneficiaries. COA never pointed out any deficiency that employees stole. There is nothing like that. And if they point it out, we will see to it that we will act on it… We have no notice of suspension. They are cross-checking the validation as well.)

Gatchalian did not deny the COA’s notice that there were times that the documents submitted by aid applicants were not thoroughly checked. State auditors found that there were some falsified medical certificates and other documents.

“Because of the grind na ang dami talagang lumalapit [due to so many people approaching us for help]. Sometimes, our social workers or development workers are also human beings na subject to human error,” Gatchalian said.

Addressing the report that there were beneficiaries who received up to P10,000 even if they were only entitled to P5,000 in the masterlist, the DSWD maintained that they could receive a maximum of P10,000 within three months.

For example, if a beneficiary asked for medical assistance, the guidelines limited it to P10,000. However, if that person died, the program also had burial assistance. The guidelines allow the issuance of both, Gatchalian explained.
The COA also raised that the DSWD gave away P14.41 million up 20,000 families that graduated from the Pantawid Pamilyang Pilipino Program.

However, Gatchalian said that just because the beneficiaries graduated from the program, it did not mean that they were no longer poor. The DSWD gave them assistance to ensure that they do not slip back into poverty.
Addressing the COA’s concern that there was an issuance of AICS during the 2025 midterm elections, Gatchalian said that there were no politics involved.

“Our social workers are professionals. Their licenses are on the line. They will not subject themselves to political pressure because they are the ones that sign the social case intake,” the DSWD Secretary said in a mix of English and Filipino. — BM, GMA News

articles.title: NBI seeks Laos cooperation in P3.5B drug smuggling investigation
articles.summary: The National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) will seek the cooperation of Laos authorities in its probe of the attempted smuggling of P3.5 billion worth of illegal drugs into the Philippines.

blocks.text: Published October 21, 2026 12:50am
The National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) will seek the cooperation of Laos authorities in its probe of the attempted smuggling of P3.5 billion worth of illegal drugs into the Philippines.
Several personalities, including Mindanao politician and former Bangsamoro Parliament member Edriezan Hadji Nasser Rimbang, have been named as people of interest in the case.
“We have sent a letter to the authorities of law so that we can have an interaction with them. This is with the help of the Department of Foreign Affairs,” NBI Director Melvin Matibag said.

Matibag said the NBI is conducting its own investigation into the attempted Laos-Philippines drug smuggling, parallel to the Philippine National Police, but maintained that the two agencies are still cooperating.
The NBI Director said agents could be sent to Laos to conduct the investigation. They are also hoping to question the suspects in the custody of the Laos authorities.
Aerosky Services Corporation, the aviation services company involved in the private plane where the illegal drugs were found, has also signified its cooperation with the NBI, Matibag said.

The NBI Director has yet to disclose whether the agency will subpoena the persons of interest previously named by the Department of Interior and Local Government, saying that their priority was speaking with the Laos authorities. —Jean Mangaluz/LDF, GMA News

articles.title: Satellite images reveal Wainwright, Alta., fire devastation
articles.summary: The charred land where a blaze ripped through a portion of CFB Wainwright and claimed the lives of four service members in Alberta on Saturday can be seen from space.

image.caption: The burned area on CFB Wainwright on Monday. (Christopher Katsarov/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Canada
The charred land where a blaze ripped through a portion of CFB Wainwright and claimed the lives of four service members in Alberta on Saturday can be seen from space.
Charred landscape following deadly blaze can be seen from space
The charred land where a blaze ripped through a portion of CFB Wainwright in Alberta on Saturday, claiming the lives of four service members and injuring dozens of others, can be seen from space.

Images from Planet Labs shows the extent of the fire, which was fuelled at least in part by dry land and howling winds. Environment Canada had issued a wind alert that morning and the fire danger index in the area was deemed extreme by Natural Resources Canada.

The images show a burnt area of roughly 10 square kilometres on Sunday, one day after the blaze was first reported. The general area of the base where the fire began is referred to as a "permanent danger area" by OpenStreetMap, a widely used geographic database maintained by volunteers.
On Sunday, the Municipal District of Wainwright reported the fire was being held.

Canadian Armed Forces Maj.-Gen. Wade Rutland, inaugural commander of the revitalized 1st Canadian Division, told reporters Sunday that the fire began as a grass fire and spread rapidly around 4 p.m. as the wind direction changed.
That day, soldiers were throwing hand grenades on a grenade range, he said, while others were conducting a "section attack," in which 10 soldiers attack a simulated enemy.

articles.title: New EU plan for Arctic warily eyes influence of Russia, US
articles.summary: The EU unveiled its priorities in the Arctic as it vies with Russia, China and the US for influence. EU foreign affairs chief Kaja Kallas said drone incursions, GPS jamming and cable sabotage…

image.caption: Greenland's melting ice sheet is a climate risk which is contributing to global sea level rise [FILE: May 5, 2021]Image: Ulrik Pedersen/NurPhoto/picture alliance

blocks.text: The EU on Tuesday presented a new Arctic Strategy that outlines the bloc's priorities in the key region amid challenges such as security threats, climate change and mining.

Russia is building up its military power in the Arctic, and US President Donald Trump has threatened Greenland, saying the Danish territory is needed for American security interests but later signed a deal with Denmark over US military access to the territory. China is also investing in the region and has shipping ambitions there.

The northern parts of Finland and Sweden, along with Greenland are located within the Arctic, meaning part of the region is in the European neighborhood. Iceland and Norway, two other Arctic states, are also involved in the European single market.
'Tectonic plates of geopolitics' colliding in Arctic
"The Arctic is one place where the tectonic plates of geopolitics are colliding," European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said.

"When we see that sovereignty, territorial integrity and the rules that have underpinned security in the region can no longer be taken for granted, we have to act and change our strategic posture," she added.
EU High Representative for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy Kaja Kallas said Russia "has reopened Soviet-era bases and is testing new weapons" in the Arctic.

"Drone incursions, GPS jamming and the sabotage of undersea cables undermine Arctic security," Kallas continued. Russia's shadow fleet, which is an attempt to circumvent Western sanctions, is active in the Arctic.

On Arctic security, the EU plans to develop a maritime security hub in the region "to facilitate information sharing form seabed to space." The bloc also intends to expand European icebreaker capacity and extend its satellite surveillance program in the region.
Russia's Arctic buildup is Iceland's security headache
However, the EU does not intend to compete with NATO in the region, EU Commissioner for International Partnerships Jozef Sikela told DW. Twenty-three EU countries are members of NATO.

"NATO will remain basically the center of defense and the center of deterrence, but NATO doesn't have a budget, the member state has," Sikela said. "This is first about the proper focus and the proper use of resources of the NATO member states and about better coordination."
EU Arctic strategy highlights security and raw materials
EU to boost climate research as Arctic faces ice melting crisis

In regard to the climate, the Arctic is warming about four times faster than the global average. The melting of ice and glaciers in the Arctic pose risks to Europe such as prolonged heatwaves, drought and flooding.
Sikela said, "Collaboration among the Arctic is very difficult," adding, "We're not getting information about the permafrost from the biggest part of the Arctic territory."

Sikela accused Russia of "unprecedented" actions in the Arctic and said the "catastrophic level of drilling and opening new mines" in the region is contributing to its rapid warming. The Arctic is rich in critical minerals and rare earth elements such as nickel.

As part of the EU Arctic Strategy, the bloc intends "to strengthen climate research, observation and monitoring" and launch flagship projects utilizing AI to "anticipate extreme weather and cascading disasters such as coastal flooding."

blocks.caption: Norway, which is not an EU member state, is home to Western Europe's largest LNG plant near the city of Hammerfest  [FILE: March 14, 2024]Image: Lisi Niesner/REUTERS

blocks.text: Although Russia and other non-EU countries such as Norway drill in the Arctic, the EU does not want to expand new drilling in the region. European Commissioner for Energy and Housing Dan Jorgensen said the EU's view "on drilling in the Arctic remains the same and it's very clear: oil, coal and gas must stay in the ground."
Greenland submarine cable route project bypasses US

Regarding economic interests in the Arctic, the bloc may take further steps to bypass the US. The strategy calls for "resilient submarine cable connectivity linking Greenland directly to Europe, with potential future extensions towards Canada and Japan."
The EU also outlined new plans regarding the residents of the Arctic region. The bloc wants to strengthen dialogue with Indigenous people along with expanding Erasmus+ opportunities for Arctic youth.

articles.title: Juror sends mysterious letter to jailed man he just helped convict of murder in Windsor, Ont.
articles.summary: Roughly two months after a first-degree murder trial in Windsor, Ont., ended, one juror took the “highly unusual” step of sending the convicted man a letter requesting to meet.

image.caption: A juror sent Glen Mayer a letter, shown in this image, while he was at Windsor, Ont.'s South West Detention Centre after he was convicted of first-degree murder of a man who'd been having an affair with his wife. (Superior Court of Justice)

blocks.text: Windsor·New
Roughly two months after a first-degree murder trial in Windsor, Ont., ended, one juror took the “highly unusual” step of sending the convicted man a letter requesting to meet.
Lawyer for Glen Mayer, guilty of killing man in wife's affair, argued letter created 'concerning dynamic'
In June, a Superior Court of Justice jury found Glen Mayer guilty of first-degree murder, which comes with an automatic life sentence and no chance of parole for 25 years.

On Monday, family members of Tony Bechara — who was shot dead in his own home on Jan. 20, 2024, after Mayer learned Bechara was having an affair with his wife — were waiting to read their victim impact statements in court prior to sentencing.

items: 'Part of my heart was taken,' mom of murdered Belle River, Ont., man tells emotional sentencing hearing

blocks.text: Instead, the defence put forward a motion requesting what’s known as a judicial inquiry based on the letter.
The typed letter, obtained by CBC News, was addressed to Mayer and requests a meeting to “perhaps discuss some things with respect to your current circumstances.”
“I have some observations I’d like to share with you as well, and I’d be interested in your feedback on those things," it reads.
The individual, whose name and contact information is redacted from the court document, didn’t include identification as a juror in the letter.
Defence wonders if verdict was 'tainted'

The trial heard that in the overnight hours of Jan. 20, 2024, Mayer found out about the affair between his wife and Bechara, left his LaSalle home with his registered handgun and drove to Belle River to confront Bechara.
Mayer testified that he and Bechara were yelling, and Bechara grabbed a knife and came toward him. That's when Mayer pulled out his gun and shot Bechara multiple times.
Hours later, Mayer turned himself in to the LaSalle police station with his dad.
Defence lawyer Julianna Greenspan says she plans to file for an appeal of the guilty verdict on behalf of Mayer. (Jason Viau/CBC)
Mayer’s defence lawyer, Julianna Greenspan, said the letter creates a “highly unusual, very concerning dynamic.”

Since both Mayer and the juror connected to the letter heard the same evidence at trial, Greenspan said, the letter raises “a concern that he’s referencing information” beyond what occurred in the courtroom.
“It does suggest on its face that there is extraneous information that this juror is wanting and hoping to share privately with Mr. Mayer,” said Greenspan.
If outside information was used by this juror, or the jury, during the trial, Greenspan argued, it could have “tainted the verdict.”
Jurors can't discuss info not shared in open court

The Criminal Code of Canada also states a juror can be found “guilty of an offence punishable on summary conviction” if the individual discloses information relating to the proceeding that wasn’t shared in open court.
"Jurors are, in the course of deliberations, to be in a private space, and that cannot be pierced," said Greenspan.

items: Man on trial for murder learns of wife's affair hours prior to shooting death of her co-worker, Crown says

blocks.text: After hearing the lawyers’ arguments for nearly two hours, Justice J. Ross Macfarlane took a 20-minute break and returned to dismiss the motion to conduct a judicial review.
He said the information presented by the defence “does not provide a credible basis that this jury may have been exposed to extraneous evidence.”

This image from surveillance video shows Mayer turning himself in to the LaSalle Police Service on Jan. 20, 2024. He was convicted of the first-degree murder of Tony Bechara. (Superior Court of Justice)
Macfarlane also asked Greenspan why she waited so long to bring the letter to the attention of the court if she had been so concerned.
The trial ended June 26 and the letter was stamped as received by the South West Detention Centre on Aug. 26.
Lawyer consulted others about unusual letter
Greenspan explained in court that given the unusual nature of this letter, she consulted with a number of individuals on the appropriate next steps.
She also indicated she reached out to the individual to confirm he in fact was a juror and attempt to suss out his intentions.

The juror responded via email to say that they have “no information or details on the aforementioned case Mr. Mayer was involved with whatsoever, other than the information I was entrusted with during my involvement as a member of that particular jury.”
The juror also said they still want a private meeting with Mayer and he’s not “requesting an audience” with lawyers present.
Greenspan said the second correspondence is more guarded and calculated compared to the first letter, and is written in a “litigator” sort of tone.
“It heightens the need for inquiry,” she said.
Within the next 30 days, Greenspan said, she intends to file for an appeal of Mayer’s guilty verdict.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Jason Viau is reporter for CBC News based in Windsor, Ont. He has an interest in telling stories related to accountability, policing, court, crime and municipal affairs. You can email story ideas and tips to jason.viau@cbc.ca.

articles.title: ‘Bad decisions’: Man convicted for taking Peachy the flamingo from Las Vegas hotel
articles.summary:
Mitchell Fairbarn found guilty of animal cruelty after prosecutors say he hurt and frightened the 27-year-old bird

A Canadian man was convicted of animal cruelty charges Monday for snatching…

blocks.text: A Canadian man was convicted of animal cruelty charges on Monday for snatching a flamingo named Peachy from its enclosure at an iconic Las Vegas hotel.
Prosecutors said it was a malicious prank while a lawyer for the tourist insisted it was drunken foolishness not meant to harm the bird.

Prosecutors said tourist Mitchell Fairbarn hurt and frightened the 27-year-old Chilean flamingo when he took it from its habitat at the Flamingo Las Vegas Hotel and Casino and carried the squawking bird to his room on 3 March. Defense attorney Josh Tomsheck told jurors at trial in a Nevada court that the man deeply regretted the “bad decisions” he made while intoxicated.
After about five hours of deliberations, jurors returned convictions on felony and misdemeanor animal cruelty counts against the Ontario, Canada, man.

Fairbarn remains under house arrest pending a sentencing hearing set for 1 December. He faces up to four years in prison for the felony and possibly six more months for the misdemeanor conviction. Following the verdict, he declined to comment as he left the courtroom with his wife. He showed no visible emotion.
His lawyer also had no comment.

After the incident, the flamingo was mostly unharmed but is more anxious and nervous when being evaluated, said Peachy’s veterinarian, Tiffany Moore, medical director of Lone Mountain Animal Hospital.

Prosecutors told jurors earlier that Fairbarn willfully caused the bird physical pain, noting feathers were found on the hotel floor. Video showed the bird squawking while Fairbarn handled it and prosecutors said Peachy felt pain when it was pulled by its feet.

Video played at the trial showed Fairbarn holding the flamingo in an elevator and carrying it down a hotel hallway at the famous hotel. The Flamingo is one of the oldest hotels on the Las Vegas Strip, and its well-known flamingo habitat also features hummingbirds, turtles, koi and other species.
Peachy was missing some feathers after being taken.

Las Vegas police responded to the scene after security staff reported that someone had taken the flamingo. When Peachy was located, it was missing seven to eight feathers, had blood on its feathers and injuries to its wings, authorities said.
Taking the bird was “dumb” and “fueled by drunkenness”, the defense attorney Tomsheck said. But he added that his client never intended any harm to the bird, a key element in the felony charge.

“He should not have done that, should not have gone into the habitat, shouldn’t have touched a bird, shouldn’t have taken Peachy inside,” Tomsheck said. “The truth is, Mitch was drunk. Mitch was stupid. He made bad decisions.”
Fairbarn could be seen in court at one point with head lowered, hands covering his eyes.

The man had received death threats after taking the flamingo, and he was unable to leave the US when his father died while Fairbarn was awaiting trial, said Haley Willming, the Clark county prosecutor. While those events were unfortunate, the prosecutor said, “none of that would have happened had he not done what he did, had he not made the choices he made”.
Jurors began deliberating shortly before midday after closing arguments on Monday morning.
Nevada animal rights advocate John Waudby, who recently helped strengthen the state’s animal cruelty laws, said he believes justice was delivered on Peachy’s behalf.
“I hope this sends a message to anybody else that wants to mess with our animals, that you’re not going to do it in Nevada,” he said outside the courtroom after Monday’s verdict.

articles.title: EDCOM 2 cites gaps in classroom allocations
articles.summary: The Second Congressional Commission on Education found gaps in the distribution of classroom allocations, with some municipalities with the largest shortages allegedly receiving fewer classrooms.

blocks.text: October 21, 2026 | 12:00am
EDCOM 2 said the issue was raised during the Oct. 16 Senate committee on finance hearing on the Department of Education (DepEd)’s proposed budget for 2027.
EDCOM 2

MANILA, Philippines — The Second Congressional Commission on Education (EDCOM 2) found gaps in the distribution of classroom allocations, with some municipalities with the largest shortages allegedly receiving fewer classrooms.

EDCOM 2 reportedly discovered that in DepEd’s 2026 classroom allocation, only 45.2 percent of the 332 local governments with the largest estimated classroom shortages were among the top recipients of planned classroom allocations.

EDCOM 2 co-chairman Sen. Bam Aquino said DepEd and the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) should accelerate classroom construction and ensure that allocations translate into completed facilities.

For this year, DepEd has initiated multiple channels to speed up classroom construction, targeting to complete 18,950 classrooms. It tapped the DPWH, partnered with provincial and city governments, civil society organizations and Public-Private Partnership Programs (PPPs).

EDCOM 2 executive director Karol Mark Yee praised DepEd for its “extraordinary efforts in mobilizing different routes for classroom construction. However, we also highlight the need for strategic and responsive allocations to ensure that these resources go where they are most needed.”

The commission reported that seven of the 10 municipalities with the highest funds for 2026 classroom construction received allocations exceeding their estimated classroom shortages based on 2023 data. Meanwhile, several municipalities with substantial deficits remained short of the classrooms needed to accommodate their learners.

“For instance, Maragondon, Cavite was allocated 272 classrooms against an estimated shortage of just 64. In contrast, Tanza, Cavite, received 448 classrooms against a shortage of a whopping 869, while Naic, Cavite was allocated 356 against a deficit of 631,” it explained.
EDCOM 2 also raised concerns over delays in classroom construction, particularly under DPWH-led implementation.

Out of the P21.45-billion allocation for 6,000 DPWH-led classrooms under the FY 2026 program, only P1.87 billion, covering 533 classrooms, allegedly reached the award or near-award stage during the hearing. Another P7 billion, covering approximately 2,000 classrooms, had been advertised for procurement.
DPWH Undersecretary Lara Esquibil pointed to failed biddings and higher construction costs amid rising fuel prices as factors affecting the implementation.
EDCOM 2 is reportedly creating a classroom tracker for transparency on where the funds are going.

For 2027, the National Expenditure Program (NEP) reportedly proposes P30.55 billion for classroom construction, with an additional request of P23.5 billion from DepEd for the construction of 2,385 new classrooms, 69 Last Mile School buildings, 500 Learning Continuity Spaces, as well as repair of 3,500 classrooms, among others. — Neil Jayson Servallos

articles.title: Prices of candles, basic goods stable ahead of Undas
articles.summary: The Department of Trade and Industry said prices of candles and other basic goods are stable ahead of the observance of All Saints’ Day and All Souls’ Day.

blocks.text: October 21, 2026 | 12:00am
Trade Secretary Cristina Roque told reporters on the sidelines of the SGV Tax Symposium yesterday that there is no movement in candle prices so far.
STAR / File
MANILA, Philippines — The Department of Trade and Industry (DTI) said prices of candles and other basic goods are stable ahead of the observance of All Saints’ Day and All Souls’ Day.
Roque said the prices of other basic necessities and prime commodities (BNPCs) also remain stable.
Apart from candles, the other BNPCs are canned sardines, canned meat, coffee, processed milk, instant noodles, condiments, laundry soap, toilet soap, salt, batteries, bottled water and bread.
So far, Roque said the DTI has not received requests for price adjustments.
“For now, no price increase,” she said.
The DTI is planning to convene a meeting with manufacturers of basic goods this week as part of the agency’s monitoring of supply and prices.
Roque said she also plans to visit facilities of sardine and meat firms.
Earlier this month, Roque visited the facility of Nature’s Spring-maker Philippine Spring Water Resources Inc. to check the supply of bottled water in the midst of El Niño.
“For those that are part of the BNPC, we want to check the supply. And then we also want to check their inventory,” she said.
“But for now, there’s no need to panic. The prices of BNPCs within the list of the DTI are stable,” Roque said.

articles.title: Philippines retains Tier 1 status in human trafficking report
articles.summary: The Philippines has maintained its Tier 1 ranking for the 11th consecutive year in the US State Department’s 2026 Trafficking in Persons Report, highlighting sustained government efforts to…

blocks.text: October 21, 2026 | 12:00am

The development was announced at a briefing by Interior and Local Government Undersecretary for Peace and Order Nestor Sanares, who also leads the country’s Senior Officials Meeting on Transnational Crime (SOMTC).

MANILA, Philippines — The Philippines has maintained its Tier 1 ranking for the 11th consecutive year in the US State Department’s 2026 Trafficking in Persons (TIP) Report, highlighting sustained government efforts to prevent human exploitation, prosecute traffickers and protect victims.

Sanares pointed out that the Tier 1 status, the highest rating given by the US State Department, indicates that the Philippines fully meets the minimum international standards for the elimination of human trafficking through inter-agency coordination.

“This milestone underscores the continuing commitment of the Philippine government, through the Inter-Agency Council Against Trafficking (IACAT) and its member agencies, to strengthen prevention, victim protection, prosecution and partnership,” Sanares said.

The DILG official noted that the 2026 TIP Report credited key institutional interventions, including the mandatory nationwide rollout of a specialized Victim Identification System, an enhanced National Referral Mechanism, expanded IACAT prosecutorial task forces and the launch of the IACAT ProtectPortal.

Sanares made the announcement as the Philippines leads preparatory SOMTC sessions with the Association of Southeast Asian Nations and dialogue partners China, Japan and South Korea ahead of the 20th ASEAN Ministerial Meeting on Transnational Crime.

articles.title: Peak power demand seen rising amid El Niño
articles.summary: The country’s peak electricity demand could jump by 10.7 percent next year as the “super El Niño” threatens to further intensify summer heat, according to the Department of…

blocks.text: October 21, 2026 | 12:00am

MANILA, Philippines — The country’s peak electricity demand could jump by 10.7 percent next year as the “super El Niño” threatens to further intensify summer heat, according to the Department of Energy.
Latest DOE data showed peak demand could reach 22,231 megawatts in 2027, up from the 20,088 MW recorded earlier this year.
Peak demand refers to the highest amount of electricity needed at a given time, when households and businesses use the most power.
The DOE monitors peak demand to ensure the country has enough electricity to meet consumer needs and prevent power outages.
Despite the projected increase, Energy Undersecretary Mario Marasigan said the country would have a sufficient power supply amid the El Niño threat.
“We don’t see shortages,” Marasigan told reporters on the sidelines of the Philippine International Nuclear Energy Forum yesterday.
On the supply side, he said hydropower facilities would be the most affected by El Niño, with output potentially dropping by as much as 60 percent.
The DOE is also assessing how the climate phenomenon could affect the efficiency of solar power plants and the performance of biomass facilities.

“If there is no agriculture, there is no produce and then definitely we have no waste,” Marasigan said, referring to biomass plants that use agricultural residues and animal waste to produce heat or electricity.
This year, the DOE expects more than 2,700 MW of power projects across the country to be completed.
Another 4,758 MW in committed projects are also expected to come online next year, further boosting power supply.
According to Marasigan, the DOE’s current priority is to resolve power supply constraints in the Visayas to ensure the region can stand on its own.
“If the Visayas can meet its own demand, it will no longer need to import power or at least reduce its imports from Luzon and Mindanao,” he said.
The National Grid Corp. of the Philippines placed the Visayas grid under red alert from 5 to 6 p.m. yesterday following the forced outages of several large coal-fired power plants.
A red alert is issued when the power supply is insufficient to meet consumer demand and the grid’s regulating requirements.
Since January, the Visayas grid has recorded 45 red alerts, based on the latest industry data.
Department of Agriculture’s action plan

The Department of Agriculture has presented a consolidated P61.99-billion action plan to mitigate the anticipated effects of El Niño on the country’s food production and rural livelihoods, while acknowledging P371 million in proposed interventions that remain unfunded.

Undersecretary for Operations Roger Navarro reported the plan’s presentation to Agriculture Secretary Francisco Tiu Laurel Jr. following the National El Niño Task Force meeting presided over by President Marcos last week, according to a memorandum outlining the meeting’s highlights.
The proposed spending package includes P6.2 billion already released under the government’s UPLIFT Program.

The remaining funding requirements and unfunded interventions underscore the importance of matching preparedness plans with timely financing and implementation as the country braces for possible drought-related disruptions.

“We need to plan ahead and ensure farmers have the support they need to cope with a potentially severe El Niño, including access to drought-tolerant rice varieties and other appropriate inputs,” Laurel said.
Among the proposed interventions without funding are cloud seeding operations and measures to manage red-striped soft scale insect infestation affecting sugarcane production.
The P371-million shortfall highlights competing demands on resources as authorities seek to protect crops and sustain agricultural output.

All government agencies were directed to adopt energy- and water-conservation measures, while early procurement and possible budget realignment were encouraged, subject to applicable procurement, budgeting, accounting and auditing rules. — Josiah Antonio, Rhodina Villanueva

articles.title: ‘Kickbacks for Co, Bernardo increased under Romualdez’
articles.summary: Kickbacks for fugitive former congressman Zaldy Co and former Department of Public Works and Highways undersecretary Roberto Bernardo from flood control projects rose from 20 percent to 25 percent…

blocks.text: Headlines
October 21, 2026 | 12:00am

Former Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) Undersecretary Engr. Roberto Bernardo sheds tears as he exposes the alleged corruption involving DPWH officials during the Blue Ribbon Committee hearing on Friday, November 14, 2025.
Senate PRIB

MANILA, Philippines — Kickbacks for fugitive former congressman Zaldy Co and former Department of Public Works and Highways undersecretary Roberto Bernardo from flood control projects rose from 20 percent to 25 percent when Leyte Rep. Martin Romualdez was speaker of the House of Representatives, former DPWH district engineer Henry Alcantara revealed yesterday.

During the continuation of the hearing on Romualdez’s bail petition for his plunder case before the Sandiganbayan Third Division, Alcantara said Co determined the 20 percent kickback, which he referred to as “commitments,” during budget deliberations in 2022.
The percentage increased to 25 percent in 2023. Alcantara said he did not know why Co sought the increase.
Alcantara explained that he would contact either Co or Bernardo to request funding, with separate lists provided to each to avoid overlapping appropriations and double payment of the “commitments.”

The money came from “advance payments” made by around 12 private contractors who had allegedly been prearranged to win bidding processes conducted by the Bulacan 1st District Engineering Office, which Alcantara previously headed.
The “commitments” were based on a list of projects sent directly to Co and Bernardo for inclusion in budget deliberations at the bicameral conference committee.
Alcantara said this differed from the “regular wishlist” prepared by district engineers for endorsement to the DPWH central office and subsequent inclusion in the National Expenditure Program (NEP).

During the redirect examination by prosecutors from the Office of the Ombudsman, Alcantara confirmed that the increase in the percentage began in 2022, when the NEP for the following year was being prepared and Romualdez was already House speaker.
Alcantara also said he would ask for a two percent share from the “commitments,” a request he described as “naglalambing” or a friendly appeal.
He recalled meeting Co around September 2021, when the latter was not yet chairman of the House committee on appropriations.
Around the same time, the first batch of up to three deliveries of “commitments” was made in storage boxes to Co’s two units on the 56th floor of Horizon Homes in Bonifacio Global City.
Subsequent deliveries were sent to Co’s house in the upscale Valle Verde village, this time in suitcases containing P30 million to P40 million each.
Alcantara added that Co would pay congressmen who proposed infrastructure projects included in the NEP because their names did not appear as project proponents.
During cross-examination, defense lawyers led by Thea Daep sought to establish that Romualdez was not House speaker when the deliveries took place.
Alcantara also admitted that his judicial affidavit and testimonies at other legislative hearings on the flood control scandal did not mention Romualdez.

Asked by Moreno who was the “most intelligent guy” behind the kickback scheme, Alcantara said: “I do not know who started it. When I was an Engineer II and project engineer, this had already been a practice. I do not know who came up with it.”

articles.title: Swimmer, 65, killed in shark attack off South Africa's east coast
articles.summary: Janine Lochrenberg, 65, was out on her daily morning swim with her club when she was attacked, her family tell the BBC.

blocks.text: A South African woman has been killed in a shark attack off the country's east coast, in what is the first recorded such fatality this year.
Janine Lochrenberg was swimming off a beach in KuGompo City (formerly East London) on Tuesday morning when she was attacked.
Witnesses said the 65-year-old was bitten in two places and died before she was brought to shore.
Shark attacks are rare in South Africa, with about 10 fatal ones since 2012, according to the Florida Museum's International Shark Attack File.

Lochrenberg was out on a daily morning swim with her local open water swimming club when she was attacked at around 08:00 (06:00 GMT). Fellow swimmers brought her to shore, but it's believed she died before they could get her out of the water.
She was bitten on her thigh and her upper arm, one of her fellow swimmers told the BBC. They also said she had been wearing a magnetic shark repellent band on her ankle at the time.
Lochrenberg's sister Margot said she was holding her sister's head as they brought her to shore but believed she bled out in the water.
She told the BBC that her sister had "loved the water so much" despite knowing there was an "elevated shark presence in East London".
"She'd made peace with that. She had a deep affinity with the water and was a remarkable person," she said.
Barbara Briceland, Lochrenberg's partner, told the BBC the retired medical physicist was a good swimmer, who often swam far out into the breakers, and described her as very brave.
"She was highly intelligent, lots of fun, kind, in a quietish way, thoughtful, well-loved with a love of life."
Briceland added they were looking forward to retirement and were about to leave for a three-week road trip together.
Orient Beach, where the attack took place, has been closed alongside another nearby beach, authorities confirmed.

articles.title: Flavio Bolsonaro’s ‘corrupto’ stunt sparks viral meme before Brazil election runoff
articles.summary:
Far-right presidential candidate’s TV debate swipe at rival backfires as people take to social media to parody it

To Flávio Bolsonaro and his publicists, it must have seemed an ingenious…

blocks.text: To Flávio Bolsonaro and his publicists, it must have seemed an ingenious idea that would expose his rival’s supposed crookedness on the eve of Brazil’s presidential election.

But the far-right politician’s decision to attend a primetime television debate against his leftwing opponent, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, with the word “corrupto” (corrupt) written on the palm of his hand has backfired.
Rather than drawing attention to the incumbent’s alleged misdeeds, many of the programme’s millions of viewers sarcastically took Bolsonaro’s hand-written message as an admission of his own guilt.
Following Sunday night’s debate, Lula supporters from all walks of life have flooded social media with photographs of their own self-descriptions inked on their palms.
John Ulhoa, the guitarist from a pop rock band called Pato Fu, jokingly described himself as a “musician (and a hunk)”.
Allow Instagram content?

This article includes content provided by Instagram. We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as they may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content, click 'Allow and continue'.
The Emmy-winning comedian Antonio Tabet introduced himself to his 2.8 million followers on X as an artist.
Carlos Marcio used both palms to portray himself as a cellist and author.
Carla Emanuela Sacramento, an obstetric nurse, posted a photograph of herself clad in personal protective equipment and with the words “primary health care nurse” proudly written on her right palm.

Prominent politicians also jumped on the trend, including Lula’s health minister, the infectious disease specialist Alexandre Padilha, whose palm noted he was a doctor, and Tabata Amaral, who identified as a political scientist and astrophysicist.

All across the country, librarians, oil workers, engineers, journalists, architects, pilots, psychologists, seamstresses, street cleaners, teachers, influencers, and police officers used ballpoint pens to inscribe their professions on to their skin.
Writing on Substack, the Latin America expert James Bosworth called Bolsonaro’s stunt a “critical error” in his bid for power.

“It may have seemed like an inspired pre-debate gimmick. Instead, he gave the world a meme image that will stick with him for the rest of his political career,” Bosworth said, offering politicians a word of advice.
“Don’t write the word ‘corrupto’ on your hand and show it to the audience,” Bosworth suggested.

Bolsonaro, who is the son of the jailed former president Jair Bolsonaro, is a professional politician who has long faced corruption accusations, although he denies them and has never been convicted. The 45-year-old senator also has well-documented ties to members of Rio’s mafia underworld and once employed the relatives of the city’s most notorious contract killer, Adriano da Nóbrega. Last week two allies were arrested for alleged involvement with the Red Command drug faction, which Donald Trump recently designated a foreign terrorist organisation. Bolsonaro voiced surprise at those arrests and said the men had the right to prove their innocence.
On Monday, Brazilian media reported that Bolsonaro was being investigated by the federal police as part of a money-laundering inquiry.
Lula, whose Worker’s party (PT) has also been involved in major corruption scandals, used Sunday’s debate to throw down the gauntlet to Bolsonaro.

The leftwing incumbent said he would give electoral authorities access to his banking and phone recordings, and those of close relatives, in order to prove he was not corrupt – if Bolsonaro agreed to do the same.

Bolsonaro, who, polls suggest, holds a slender advantage ahead of Sunday’s second-round runoff, has yet to respond to Lula’s challenge. The rightwinger won the 4 October first round by more than 2m votes.

articles.title: Germany news: Hackers release AfD party emails
articles.summary: Germany's far-right AfD has launched an inquiry after the release of thousands of emails following a cyberattack. Also, investors pledged billions for Germany at a major summit in Berlin. DW has more…

image.caption: The released material reportedly included emails sent by party figures as well as bank statements, academic certificates and membership listsImage: Felix Kästle/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Published October 20, 2026last updated October 20, 2026
Far-right AfD says emails stolen in September cyberattack

Germany's far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) said on Tuesday that it was looking into the theft and subsequent online publication of emails stolen by unidentified hackers during a cyberattack last month.
An AfD spokesperson said the hackers had targeted a hosting provider used by the party and appeared to have copied data from a small number of mostly inactive email accounts.

"The recent online publication of what is presumably a portion of this data is currently being investigated," the spokesperson said. "A preliminary assessment can only be provided once this investigation has been concluded."
Although the spokesperson did not say how much data was stolen, an earlier report by the mass-circulation daily Bild put the number of AfD-linked emails published at more than 420,000.
According to Bild, the material published included not only emails sent by party figures such as co-leader Alice Weidel but also bank statements, academic certificates and membership lists.
The website hosting the material was offline by Tuesday afternoon.
However, archived versions showed a volume of 281 gigabytes of data under the headline "The party's own records, unedited."
The emails and other materials published have not yet been certified as authentic by any independent body.

The AfD, several state chapters of which have been classified as "confirmed right-wing extremist" by regional branches of Germany's domestic intelligence agency, has been topping recent national opinion polls and made gains in recent state elections.
Some politicians and civil society groups have called for it to be banned, arguing that the party is a threat to democracy, an accusation the party has rejected.
